topics.title: [marin] Keep Kueue-gated serve tasks in the placement budget
topics.body:
## tl;dr summary

Agent found an issue when doing evals; the `SchedulingGated` state from Kueue -> `BUILDING` in Iris -> `marin.inference.iris` during evals started its 2400s startup budget. But it shouldn't count as startup time since it's still queued. 

## Agent Explanation
Iris reports a Pending pod as BUILDING, including a pod that Kueue still holds at its admission gate (status message `SchedulingGated: ...`). The eval runner's endpoint wait in `marin.inference.iris` counted BUILDING as placed, so the 2,400 s startup budget ran while the serve job was still queued for GPUs. Eight eval groups failed this way in one night with no GPU allocated.

A BUILDING task whose status message starts with `SchedulingGated` now counts as queued. The 4 h placement budget covers gated time, and the startup budget starts only once the gate is lifted. A preemption requeue still resets the startup budget. The wait now reads per-task status with `list_tasks` because the job-level state counts do not carry the status message.

A pod that Kueue has admitted but the scheduler reports `Unschedulable` still counts as placed, so the startup budget bounds an admitted pod that does not start. `Unschedulable` can mean a bad resource request or ordinary capacity or affinity limits; this keeps the existing behavior for both.

Separate from #10030 / #10033.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: [inference] Start serve readiness timeout after placement
topics.body:
Start the serve readiness timeout when a task's current attempt has an assigned Iris worker or a node-bound Kubernetes pod, or when the task is running. Kubernetes reports Kueue-gated Pending pods as BUILDING; the previous state-count check treated them as placed and failed evaluations after 2,400 seconds without allocating a GPU. Federated task status can also show a peer display label as its worker ID before placement, so the waiter uses the current attempt's assignment.

Queued time remains subject to the four-hour placement deadline. Requeued attempts stop consuming the startup budget, and old attempts' placement details do not mark the new attempt as placed.

Fixes #10036

topics.title: [levanter] Exclude cache markers from Hugging Face mirrors
topics.body:
Skip a Hugging Face repository file when its name matches the configured cache completion marker. The DARE-TIES-02 repository contains `.cache_metadata.json` from its Base cache. topics.title: Validate localized online feedback for tool-use failures
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Final-token preference optimization (FTPO) reduced repeated tool-call opening markers from 72/156 to 1/156 on a frozen-prefix diagnostic, a 98.6% reduction. Valid first-call syntax increased from 21/156 to 42/156. The selected checkpoint improved standalone BFCL-Parity/Pi from 30/123 to 43/123, while IFBench Loose declined from 82/300 to 78/300. These are single-sample validation results; capability preservation remains unproven.

The campaign is complete. The [selected checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Protocol-FTPO/tree/d761ea0a94500c2aa24aa4cd71b5a149d962e5c8) is public. The [exact benchmark](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Tool-Protocol-Replay-v1) remains private pending clarification of redistribution rights for captured client-supplied instructions and tool descriptions. An inaccessible link for an unauthenticated reader is expected. This precaution is not a finding that the captured text is confidential or that its capture violated any terms.

## Description and hypothesis

BFCL is the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard. BFCL-Parity is this campaign's fixed 123-task panel, audited against the full task set by the [partition code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py); its task identities are in the private benchmark manifest. Pi is the agent harness that executes model tool calls. Harbor manages task/agent integration, and Daytona supplies task containers. DPO means direct preference optimization; SFT means supervised fine-tuning.

The preceding BFCL campaign's extended DPO run degraded Pi task success from 34/123 to 0/123 after eight updates. That observation motivated testing a much narrower training signal. This experiment asks whether changing a preference at one observed invalid token boundary can reduce a recurring tool-protocol error while retaining task capability. It does not establish the cause of the earlier DPO collapse. Related work: [BFCL closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040), [localized feedback proposal #9691](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691), and [FTPO implementation #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887).

The implemented target is a second `<tool_call>` immediately after an already-opened call, allowing intervening JSON whitespace. The experiment narrowed the original closure proposal to this repeated-opener case. General closing-token repairs, short repair spans, off-top-K verified alternatives, masked-SFT comparisons, and cross-harness transfer remain follow-up work.

## Benchmark design and construction

The source BFCL revision is `6bedd7878dc5d6f3456b4d80b781eb3c2d84f262`. Its campaign partition has 3,518 training-approved task identities and a separate 123-task BFCL-Parity panel. Before failure selection, task IDs were sorted by SHA-256 of `repeated-opener-v1:<task_id>`; the first 704 were reserved for diagnostics and the other 2,814 for this intervention's training.

The builder scanned 717 of 718 retained trajectory archives and examined 5,771 records on reserved tasks. One archive was excluded for disagreement between literal opener strings and special-token positions. It excluded 857 candidate prefix occurrences over the 24,576-token limit, then selected the lexicographically smallest eligible prefix hash per task. This produced 156 unique task prefixes of 10,101–24,558 tokens. A separate training partition supplied 581 replay prefixes. No diagnostic or parity task entered this FTPO training set.

Training selection used the same source-archive set and repeated-opener extraction rule, restricted to training task IDs. It examined 22,003 training records, found 14,761 within-budget candidate occurrences, and excluded 2,880 oversized occurrences and two audited token-alignment failures. Selection kept the smallest prefix hash per task, then removed nine selected prefixes that failed the runtime boundary-selector check. The final 581 prefixes represent 581 distinct tasks. Archive overlap is expected; task identities are disjoint. See [training construction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/skill_acquisition/training_data.py).

Each diagnostic retains exact model-input token IDs through an initial opener, immediately before a historical repeated opener at the first malformed call in an assistant span outside thinking. Historical source identity: `users/benfeuer/inputs/bfcl-rl-recovered-policy@2026.10.04.26:479563dc`. The selected prefixes contain its prior conversation and harness context. New continuations are generated from the evaluated policy. The source model is distinct from the later Recovery initializer.

The case-file SHA-256 is `9249b4a7f25d45ab6884c152cd6d975d71312e0c8ba1ecf29bf0cffaea62d8ed`. The Recovery tokenizer SHA-256 is `6a61ca2105a54e9984169b409581f31cc50330d1b47104af13c221b05e462e45`. The private dataset includes cases, construction code, manifest, exclusions, scorer, usage instructions, and aggregate/per-case diagnostic labels. Training data remains private.

This is a failure-enriched validation set repeatedly used during development and selection. It is not an untouched test or representative BFCL sample. Task-ID separation does not establish absence from the initializer's earlier training; original source records lack task-content hashes. The frozen histories were collected under an earlier harness, whereas live task evaluation uses Pi. No cross-harness learning claim follows from that combination.

## Online training protocol

All completed candidates start independently from [Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery/tree/850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83), the prior BFCL `.304/hf/step-1` export, with a frozen reference. The selected run is `2026.10.12.2`, export `global_step_4`; suffixes identify dated run versions, not numbers of optimizer updates.

The loop samples fresh continuations from historical training-only prefixes. At most one repeated-opener boundary per response supplies a target. The rejected token is the repeated opener. Accepted alternatives must be among the captured top-20 candidates and decode to `{` after whitespace trimming. Candidate filtering uses relative `min_p=0.01` and at most 20 accepted tokens. A legal opening brace does not prove that the remaining call will be valid. Empty-target batches skip the optimizer.

FTPO applies a selected-position logit-margin preference loss. For chosen-minus-rejected logit difference `d`, its margin-2 term is `softplus(2-d) * clamp((2-d)/2, 0, 1)`, averaged over accepted alternatives. Frozen-reference squared-logit regularization uses `lambda_mse=0.4`, targeted-token `lambda_mse_target=0.05`, and target deadband `tau_mse_target=0.5`. Token-frequency balancing strengths are 0.3 for rejected tokens and 0.5 for chosen tokens. The pinned implementation defines masking and global weighted normalization. The stronger-regularization run changes `lambda_mse` to 0.8.

No critic, learned reward model, or PPO task-reward objective is used. Fresh generation makes the continuations on-policy; the conditioning histories remain fixed historical replays. This is not full multi-turn on-policy task training. A one-token supervision target still requires model forward/backward computation and changes shared parameters.

| Setting | Executed configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Optimizer | AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 0.5 |
| Learning rate | Constant `4e-6`; runs `2026.10.12.3` and `.4` use `2e-6`; no warmup |
| Batch | 16 prompts, 2 continuations each, one update epoch; train/forward microbatch 2 |
| Allocation | 192 H100s: policy 120, reference 64, inference 8 |
| Parallelism | Policy pipeline 15 × expert 8; reference pipeline 8 × expert 8; TP/CP/SP 1, no packing |
| Generation | Seed 42, temperature 1, top-p 1, 8,192 new tokens; 73,728-token serving window |
| Diagnostic stop | `</tool_call>` retained in output; special tokens retained; no constrained decoding |
| Evaluation cadence | Initial, every two configured steps, and final; one-step smokes also evaluate at step 1 |
| Live task harness | Pi 0.87.0, chat-template thinking format, Daytona, 32 concurrent trials; 2 CPU/4 GiB RAM/10 GiB disk; trial timeout 1,800 seconds, verifier 300 seconds |

Raw-token protocol replay needs no container. Live BFCL/Pi task evaluation uses Daytona. Checkpoint step numbers must be distinguished from applied updates: the selected four-step run applied three updates and skipped one zero-signal batch.

The replay diagnostic uses temperature 1, top-p 1, seed 42, and an 8,192-token budget, with exactly one fresh continuation per prefix at each checkpoint. Training uses two continuations per prompt. “Single-sample” refers to one evaluated continuation per case, without repeated-generation uncertainty measurement.

Exact retained configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4 and https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. These include source, resolved launch, and captured live-resolved files, with byte hashes and caveats about historical storage paths and attempt IDs. Runtime defaults absent from YAML are listed in the gist README and pinned source. Private data and cluster dependencies prevent a public one-command rerun.

## Results measurement

The protocol diagnostic assigns the first applicable category: repeated opener, malformed JSON, invalid generic call envelope, missing/misplaced closer, or valid first-call syntax. The envelope requires a nonempty string `name` and object-valued `arguments`. This does not check tool availability, its argument schema, execution, or later calls. The packaged scorer independently reproduced all 468 retained diagnostic labels at selected-run steps 0, 2, and 4.

| Selected run, configured step | Repeated opener | Malformed JSON | Invalid envelope | Missing/misplaced closer | Valid |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 72 | 27 | 23 | 13 | 21 |
| 2 | 11 | 47 | 47 | 17 | 34 |
| 4 | 1 | 58 | 42 | 13 | 42 |

Among the 72 cases initially labeled repeated opener, final labels were 12 valid, 36 malformed JSON, 19 invalid envelope, four missing/misplaced closer, and one repeated opener. Every one of those 19 invalid envelopes lacked `arguments`. Many malformed responses still contain repeated marker-like content or `$LANG`. Reducing the first visible error does not imply a complete repair.

Standalone exported-checkpoint evaluation measures BFCL-Parity/Pi task success, MATH-500 accuracy, HumanEval+ pass@1, and IFBench loose-prompt accuracy. The full panel sizes are 123, 500, 164, and 300. Serving and evaluation configs are held constant across the baseline and final candidates except checkpoint identity. Inline BFCL trials are separate samples with explicit unscored cases; they are not substituted for standalone results.

| Model/run | BFCL-Parity/Pi | MATH-500 | HumanEval+ | IFBench Loose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Recovery baseline | 30/123 (24.39%) | 457/500 (91.4%) | 52.44% | 82/300 (27.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.1` | 44/123 (35.77%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 73.78% | 72/300 (24.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.2`, released | 43/123 (34.96%) | 461/500 (92.2%) | 68.90% | 78/300 (26.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.3` | 32/123 (26.02%) | 464/500 (92.8%) | 69.51% | 79/300 (26.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.4` | 37/123 (30.08%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 70.73% | 84/300 (28.00%) |

All standalone cases in this table were scored. For the released checkpoint, six MATH responses had no extractable answer and scored zero; BFCL recorded no errors. Run `.4` had two BFCL agent timeouts scored as failures and two unanswered MATH cases scored zero. Infrastructure exceptions in inline trials remain unscored and visible in the results tracker.

## Decision log and limitations

Integration attempts exposed dependency bootstrapping, microbatch, timeout, raw-token response, installed-tool wrapping, text-block grading, zero-update checkpoint, export, and invalid-argument transcript issues. Their configs and results remain in the tracker. Six completed learning candidates followed: two one-update smokes, a two-update run, the selected four-step run, a lower-rate run, and a stronger-reference-penalty run. They are not independent-seed replications.

The selected run met the campaign's 90% repeated-opener reduction target. Run `.4` reached 84.7%, with 28 valid first calls versus `.2`'s 42 and lower BFCL success, although `.4` outperformed `.2` on all three ancillary benchmarks. This motivated selecting `.2`. The two-update `.1` had the highest standalone BFCL score but only 81.7% opener reduction and the largest IFBench Loose decline among these candidates. The separate tracker gives each candidate's configured steps, applied updates, learning rate, and regularization.

IFBench Loose became the primary IF measure after trace inspection showed sensitivity to formatting and checker behavior; Strict remains a secondary measurement. This metric change occurred during the study and is not preregistered. Some strict failures reflect genuine instruction violations; others expose weak or mismatched validators. Loose does not remove all those defects. The IF follow-up preserves the original measurements and proposes an independently validated benchmark.

No repeated-generation unchanged-model control, masked-SFT arm, cross-harness transfer panel, or independently measured production tensor/logit equivalence was completed. Capability non-inferiority margins were not specified or demonstrated. Weight publication verified export bytes and all 39 weight shards; that is distinct from proving training/inference numerical equivalence. Some W&B runs report stale or crashed status despite successful Iris completion and retained final traces; the results use retained artifacts and actual-update evidence.

## Code and artifacts

Result posts: [figure and private-benchmark access](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124431515); [complete retained-results tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124432248).

- Marin [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) contains the campaign; stacked [#10058](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10058) contains closeout/review fixes. Both are open at publication. The selected run used Marin `3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6`; later code fixes must not be treated as part of that executed revision.
- MarinSkyRL merged changes: [#887 FTPO](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887), [#970 DPO/validation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/970), [#971 installed-agent engine integration](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/971), [#972 Daytona credentials](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/972), [#973 replay sessions](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/973), [#974 repeated-opener target](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/974), [#975 boundary selection](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/975), [#976 raw token prefixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/976), [#977 tool normalization](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/977), [#978 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/978), [#979 training replay/checkpoint fixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/979), and [#980 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/980).
- Harbor merged changes: [#255 native exact-token capture](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/255), [#256 correlation IDs](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/256), [#257 proxy cleanup](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/257). The configs specify executed dependency pins; these links include supporting and later closeout changes.
- Final training runtime: [MarinSkyRL `37ec019`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b). Capability evaluator: [Evalchemy `97fffeb`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/tree/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5). No new Evalchemy change is claimed for this campaign.
- Public aggregate evidence and figure: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Protocol-FTPO-Results/tree/a7bbbfbe05e16ee5cadbbcdd8135fbf59b40cfb7. Exact configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4; integration attempts: https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. The benchmark link above requires access. Raw replay prefixes and training data are not included in the public artifacts.
- Follow-ups: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060 and https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061.

## Conclusion

This run supports a narrow result: a selected-position preference intervention can sharply reduce a repeated-opener signature on fixed held-out-from-this-training histories. Most responses still fail full first-call syntax, and capability preservation is unproven. The campaign closes with a public checkpoint, public measurements, and a private reproducibility dataset. Remaining experiments are tracked in the linked follow-ups; closing this issue does not assert that all original proposal criteria were met.

<details>
<summary>Original proposal, preserved for scope comparison</summary>

Design, implement, execute, and validate online feedback loops that target specific model failures at the smallest justified token or action span. Start with tool-call closure: after a complete valid payload, prefer a harness-accepted closing sequence over an observed invalid continuation. An open but still-valid prefix is not a failure.

The BFCL recovery campaign's extended DPO run fell from 34/123 successful Pi trials to 0/123 after eight updates. Whole-trajectory preferences did not preserve tool behavior. [Public analysis and artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b).

Reuse the online final-token preference optimization (FTPO) path in [MarinSkyRL #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) where appropriate. [Dr. Doom](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) demonstrated reduced repetitive tails, but its alternative-token selection does not verify tool repairs. FTPO already supplies exact-token candidates, a selected-position preference objective, frozen-reference logit regularization, and empty-window optimizer skipping. Its supported topology excludes TP>1, context parallelism, sequence parallelism, and packing.

Done when:

- Define separate failure predicates and positive-evidence requirements for closure, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement and validate closure first; mark the other behaviors as separate subsequent experiments rather than blending them into one reward.
- Preserve the exact conditioning tokens, harness/tool schema, model version, and verification evidence. A positive candidate must be valid under the same prefix. Admit verified candidates outside rollout top-K; support a short span when a delimiter is multi-token.
- Connect on-policy generation, target construction, actual optimizer updates, weight synchronization, and fresh generation in MarinSkyRL. Reuse existing roles/checkpointing; no critic or learned reward model is required for parser-verifiable cases.
- Run a Pi-only smoke and a bounded learning experiment on training-complement tasks. Compare local preference learning with positive-only masked SFT on the same repairs and an unchanged-model control. Record skipped versus applied updates and compute costs.
- Evaluate held-out protocol validity, accepted/executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate before and after training. Evaluate other harnesses to measure transfer; do not infer transfer from Pi alone. Keep BFCL-Parity out of mined training targets.
- Publish pinned configuration, provenance, failure examples cleared for redistribution, and results including regressions. State that token-local supervision changes shared model weights and does not guarantee globally local effects or one-token compute cost.

[Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [datakit local-pair mining #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041). [Detailed proposed interventions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-repair-versus-online-rl-20261011.md).

</details>

topics.title: [canary-datakit-smoke] Store starves at one worker and times out
topics.body:
The tier-1 Datakit smoke ferry exceeded the 7,100-second Actions wait while `datakit/store` was still processing. The store requested 106 map workers; Iris ran one and left 105 pending. The root job had no task failures and was still running at 15:25 UTC.

Reproduce:
1. Run `.github/workflows/marin-canary-datakit-tier1.yaml` with the current `TIER1_SCALE` in `experiments/ferries/datakit_ferry.py`.
2. During `datakit/store`, inspect the clustered-store worker job under the ferry job. This run showed `pending=105 running=1`; `iris_monitor.py wait --timeout 7100` then raised `TimeoutError`.

Expected: the store gets enough workers to finish the ferry within the CI wait budget, or the run reports a placement failure before that deadline.

The coordinator reported `87/106 complete, 1 in-flight, 18 queued, 1/1 workers alive, 0 dead` at 15:18:57 UTC, when Actions timed out. The only running store worker was on a `v5e` TPU VM in `us-west4`; its request was 4 CPU, 32 GiB RAM, and 64 GiB disk. The configured CPU fallback has 16 GB RAM, so it cannot host this worker shape. The uploaded controller log shows the `us-west4` v5e pool scaling at 15:18 UTC. The specific placement verdict for the other 105 workers was unavailable; Iris showed no task events for a pending worker.

## Canary run context

- Lane: `datakit-smoke`; date: 2026-10-11 UTC
- Iris job: `/runner/iris-run-job-20261011-132010`
- [Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/38142720107) and [uploaded diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/38142720107/artifacts/11705653562)
- [W&B run URL](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/datakit-smoke-38142720107-1) (`datakit-smoke-38142720107-1`)

<details>
<summary>Exact checks</summary>

```text
15:18:57 Actions: TimeoutError after 7100.0s waiting for /runner/iris-run-job-20261011-132010
15:18:57 Finelog log: [stage0-Map] 87/106 complete, 1 in-flight, 18 queued, 1/1 workers alive, 0 dead
15:23:24 Iris worker job: Tasks 0/106 completed; pending=105, running=1
15:25:17 Iris root job: running, failures=0, preemptions=0
```

Finelog query: `marin` deployment, `log` namespace, exact coordinator attempt key, `epoch_ms` from 2026-10-11 15:18:30 to 15:19:05 UTC. The queried rows were present in the hub; recent forwarding can lag. The `zephyr.execution` record confirms 106 input shards. This is an infra/scheduling timeout, with the exact pending placement cause still unconfirmed.
</details>

topics.title: [grafana] Alert on failed hero attempts during retry initialization
topics.body:
An unexpected failure of a hero training attempt can be followed by an Iris retry without a critical Grafana alert during the interruption. `TrainingProgressStalled` resets its clock for the new execution and allows 45 minutes for initialization. `TrainingTelemetryGone` stops firing when the retry publishes `phase=initializing`. The warning-only `task_retried` check requires fresh training telemetry and an event from the last 15 minutes, so it can miss a retry that takes longer to initialize.

A [September 30 checkpoint failure](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/570) resumed training about 27 minutes after the last completed step. Neither critical rule fired during that gap. The checkpoint failure's initiating cause remains unconfirmed.

Done when: an unexpected failed attempt or retry of an enrolled hero run produces a critical alert during the interruption, including while its replacement initializes. Cover retry, recovery, and duplicate-notification behavior in tests.

topics.title: [datakit] Release the shared Zephyr pool after its last stage
topics.body:
Release the shared Zephyr pool when its last stage succeeds, so idle shared workers stop holding hosts needed by dedicated pools. `run_reference_steps` runs normalization before starting the shared pool; a watcher thread calls `ZephyrContext.shutdown()` after every step in `DatakitSteps.shared_pool_steps` succeeds. All three ferries use this path through `run_reference_ferry`, as does `reference_pipeline.py --target all`. The shared pool uses `_IdleWorkerPolicy.RETAIN`, so it previously kept every acquired worker until the DAG ended: up to 512 workers (2 CPU / 16 GiB each) on v5e hosts, while the embed, quality, fuzzy-cluster, and store pools waited for hosts.

Reduce the tier-1 store worker from 4 CPU / 32 GiB RAM / 64 GiB disk to 2 CPU / 8 GiB RAM / 16 GiB disk. A store task with one normalized shard peaks below 2 GiB RAM and spills below 1 GiB. On 2026-10-12, the old shape received 1 of 106 workers; the new shape received 12 workers in 1 minute.

On the fixed code, tier 1 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153556`) succeeded in 56 minutes. Tier 3 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153605`) succeeded, and its shared pool stopped at 19:30 UTC after fuzzy dedup. Tier 3 took 5h47m, exceeding the 20,700-second CI wait. On a busy cluster, the shared pool received only 275 of its 512 workers, and tokenization took 2h37m, compared with 37 minutes on 2026-10-05.

The tier-3 fuzzy-cluster workers drop from 16 CPU / 128 GiB / 64 GiB disk to 8 CPU / 64 GiB / 32 GiB, with 64 instead of 32 workers, so the task count stays at 512. Only one of the larger workers fits on a v5e host. On 2026-10-13 the verify workers waited 3h46m for hosts, and the tier-3 ferry took 7h30m. At 16 tasks per worker, cluster text peaked at 66 GiB and verify at 26 GiB.

The three tiers passed in CI on this branch. Tier 1 took 56 minutes, and tier 2 took 1h51m. Tier 3 (`/runner/iris-run-job-20261013-165715`) took 2h25m, with 36 minutes for fuzzy verification. This is much less than the 20,700-second CI wait.

The tier concurrency groups now include `github.ref`, so a run started on a branch and the scheduled run on main do not cancel each other.

Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10047. Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10059.
topics.head: 8a683814d0d5fd4050dcd44a34ecd07549855717

topics.title: [zephyr] Cap native thread pools at the worker's and task's CPU share
topics.body:
Native thread pools (Polars, OpenMP for faiss/torch/numba/Arrow, OpenBLAS,
MKL, numba, rayon for HF tokenizers) size themselves from the node's core
count and read their cap once, at import or first pool use. An Iris task pod
on CoreWeave carries only a CPU request, so a 2-CPU Zephyr worker starts
pools sized for the whole node. The four InlineRunner stages (embed, quality
score, centroid sample, domain assign) run inside the worker actor process,
where polars/pyarrow/numpy are imported before any task runs, so nothing
inside a task can lower the cap. Today only SubprocessRunner children are
capped, and only for Polars.

`memory_budget.native_thread_env(cpu)` returns `POLARS_MAX_THREADS`,
`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`,
`NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` and `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`, each `max(1, ceil(cpu))`. It is
applied at the two boundaries that are pre-import by construction:

- the Iris environment of the coordinator and worker actor-group jobs, via a
  new optional `environment` keyword on fray `create_actor_group` (forwarded
  by the Iris backend, ignored by `LocalClient`, whose actors are threads);
- the SubprocessRunner child env, which now carries the full map at task cpu
  instead of `POLARS_MAX_THREADS` alone. Arrow in shard children stays
  API-pinned to 1.

No process writes `os.environ`, and no threads or buffers are added, so
memory can only fall. `thread_cap_environment` passes `workspace=os.getcwd()`
only because `EnvironmentConfig` requires a workspace or an image;
`convert_environment` reads only `env_vars`. Narrowing the fray keyword to
`env_vars: dict[str, str]` would drop that placeholder at the cost of
diverging from `JobRequest.environment`; happy to switch if preferred.

## Measurements

Proxy kernels standing in for each stage, on a 16-CPU VM with no CPU quota:
8 fresh 2-CPU-shaped processes at once, 3 repeats, median, clean environment
vs `native_thread_env(2)`:

| kernel | wall p50 | CPU-s per repeat | max RSS | involuntary ctx switches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| assign (faiss) | 68.8 -> 11.8 s | 1082 -> 181 | flat | 10.7M -> 10k |
| embed (numba + OpenBLAS) | 21.7 -> 21.0 s | 303 -> 274 | -300 MB | -65% |
| reader (Arrow) | 7.7 -> 7.65 s | 73 -> 68 | -57 MB | -83% |
| shuffle (Polars) | 8.6 -> 7.9 s | 124 -> 110 | -840 MB | -94% |

The capped version lands within noise of pinning each process to 2 cores
with `taskset` on every kernel. Under a `CPUQuota=200%` cgroup (GCP
preemptible shape) assign and embed gain the same; shuffle is flat because
Polars already sizes from the quota. One process alone on an idle 16-core
box is slower (2 threads instead of 16), a shape no production worker has;
the same process under a 2-CPU quota is 63% (assign) and 57% (embed) faster.
Result hashes are identical in every arm.

A local datakit pipeline under SubprocessRunner (task cpu 1 and 2.5, main vs
branch) is byte-identical with worker mem_peak ratio 1.004 and 1.001.
Fresh-interpreter probes under `native_thread_env(2)` show every covered
library reporting 2 threads.

Not measured: the CoreWeave pod shape (CPU request only, no `limits.cpu` or
cpuset) is read from the Iris k8s backend
(`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py`), not observed on a
cluster, and the stage-level production gain is extrapolated from the
kernels.

Out of scope: quality score (XLA's CPU pool ignores all six variables and
needs sched affinity), tokenizer parallelism in shard children
(`TOKENIZERS_PARALLELISM=false` stays), the store worker's
partition-process Arrow pin, and `pa.io_thread_count`.

## Tests

- SubprocessRunner map returns `pl.thread_pool_size() == ceil(task cpu)` on
  a cpu=4 worker (1 -> 1, 2.5 -> 3).
- A fresh interpreter under `native_thread_env(1.5)` reports Polars and Arrow
  pools of 2.
- The fray Iris backend submits explicit env vars merged over device
  defaults.
- A `requires_cluster` test observes (2, 2) from an inline stage on a cpu=2
  Iris worker.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the build step DAG and its memo store
topics.body:
Add the author and build stages of Taskforge as `stage30_author` and `stage40_build`. An author writes async steps decorated with `@rl_env_build_step`, which takes a step's inputs from its parameters after the context, and a final step decorated with `@rl_env_build_sink`, which reads its inputs the same way and refuses any return annotation other than `TaskSpec`. `rl_env_build_program(*steps, sink=...)` orders the steps by Kahn's algorithm, breaking ties by declaration order and running the sink last. It refuses duplicate names, unknown inputs, cycles, a step taking the sink as an input, and a step whose output reaches neither another step nor the sink, since that output would never enter the task. A step receives an `RLEnvBuildContext` (item id, model, sampling policy) and then its inputs by name, where a parameter called `proposal` receives the caller's proposal, an opaque JSON value at this point in the stack. `static_author` hands back a hand-written program as an author. `run_program` returns the sink's `TaskSpec`, and `run_build` writes it to `draft/task.json` with an `ItemBuildProvenance` in `draft/provenance.json`, which lists every step's stored memo beside that build's hit or miss status for it. The status belongs to the build and stays out of the stored memo, which the store writes only on a miss.

Each step's output is memoized under a key of `SDK_VERSION`, the sha256 of the step's own source, the content digest of each declared input, and a model digest over the model id and the sampling policy. Because inputs enter the key by content, a step that reruns with an identical output leaves its consumers cached. A helper read from outside a step body is not in the key, so changing one needs a declared input or an `SDK_VERSION` bump. Item ids belong to the caller and are only checked for file safety.

The store is a hand-rolled memo of about 60 lines over rigging's `StoragePath` and `atomic_rename`, holding content-addressed JSON blobs and per-item memos under a local path or an object-store URL. joblib keys on function identity and clears a function's whole cache when its code changes, so it reuses nothing across program revisions, and Marin's `StepSpec` hashes no code and costs a status file and a distributed lock per step. Its `load` and `store` take a caller-built key, and `memoized` is the one call the runner and a driver use, so a driver can memoize a helper against the same store with a key it builds. `memoized(store, name, key, output_type, compute)` loads under such a key and on a miss awaits `compute` and stores the result, and `run_program` calls it for every step.

Stage packages are numbered by tens in pipeline order (proposal 10, triage 20, author 30, build 40), and `tests/test_imports.py` fails when a stage imports a higher-numbered one.

The design comes from draft #9993. Later PRs bring back the proposal package, the ledger, the author's programs written by the language model, the validate and review stages, and the stage coordinator.

topics.title: [grug] Add a separate QK multiplier for hero global layers
topics.body:
Add `GrugModelConfig.qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra Q multiplier on the hero's global layers (every `global_every`-th layer and the last: full causal, RoPE disabled). Global layers multiply Q by `qk_mult` and then by `qk_mult_long_scale`. Local sliding-window layers use `qk_mult` alone. The field, its 1.0 default, and the order of the two multiplies match `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/model.py` and the pinned vLLM GrugMoE backend, which reads the same config key. A scale of 1.0 adds no op, so the live hero and existing checkpoints trace unchanged. Otherwise the layer scan's traced `is_global` flag selects the scale with `jnp.where`, which keeps one scan body for all layers and covers both RoPE paths.

Q and K are RMS-normalized, so the Q multiplier sets the softmax temperature. Moving the hero from 4K to 16K context leaves the local layers' 2048-token window unchanged, so the YaRN-style mscale, 1.3 × (0.1·ln(s) + 1), applies only to the global layers. Trial arms can raise the global scale and hold the local layers at 1.3: a long scale of 1.1386 gives 1.48, and 1.2964 gives 1.68.

The HF config export writes `qk_mult_long_scale`. A config without the key loads with 1.0. `launch_diagnostics.py` takes `--qk-mult-long-scale`. `launch_scaling_ladder.py` and `trigger_hero.sh` are unchanged because #9689 also changes them; the production flag will follow after it lands.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the stage coordinator over the build DAG
topics.body:
Add `stage_coordinator`, which runs an item through triage, author, build, validate and review with the stage functions a caller passes in `StageFunctions`. Each stage returns an event with an exit, and a transition table gives the next stage. The item's state is a fold over its events (`derive_state`). `ItemBudget` bounds build revisions and validation retries, and the coordinator spends them when it records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, `BUILD_FAILED` or `DECIDED`. A build error from the program's own code, `BuildFailure` or any other exception, costs a revision. `BuildInfrastructureFailure` (the build host failed: a sandbox did not start, an image did not pull, a pod died), `ModelUnavailable` and `OSError` (a storage fault, a missing blob or memo) are failures the author cannot fix. Those fail the item in place at the build stage, and the next `run_item` builds the same program again with its revisions unspent. When the author raises `StructuredOutputError` because its structured reply stayed invalid after the repair turn, as when the output limit cut it, the coordinator records `AUTHOR_FAILED`, spends a revision from the same budget, and asks the author again with `Revision(AUTHOR_FAILURE, ...)`.

The `OPENED` event records the digests of the proposal and the budget, and the coordinator's model digest, the model part of every step key. A relaunch with any of them changed raises `ValueError`, so every build of an item runs under one model. The author returns an `AuthoredProgram`, the program with the Python source it came from. The coordinator writes the source to `rounds/<n>/authored/<k>/program.py`, beside the manifest `program.json`, with `k` the item's build failures so far. The build stage loads the program from that file with `StageFunctions.load_program`, so a sampling model author is called once per revision. Each author call gets its own directory, so a process killed after re-authoring leaves the program of the saved `AUTHORED` event in place for the relaunch. `stage30_author/loader.py` is the plain loader; the author PR replaces it with a restricted one (allowed imports, safe builtins). A program defined in Python, as `static_author` returns, has no source, and for it the build stage asks the author again. In both cases a build whose program digest differs from the `AUTHORED` event raises.

Events stay in an `ItemEventLog` (in memory here) while the item runs. When the item reaches a terminal, `run_item` saves the log through an `ItemEventStore`. `JsonEventStore` writes `items/<item_id>/events.json` after every other file of the item, and the next `run_item` with an empty log restores the log from it. An accepted or rejected item then returns without running a stage or writing a byte. When the store lacks the final log, as after a failed save retried with the same in-memory log, `run_item` saves it before returning. An abandoned item re-enters validation with its retries reset, and a failed item resumes at the stage that raised, with the step store under `<root>/store` serving the build steps already run. A process killed mid-item restarts from the last saved terminal, or from triage. The ledger PR adds a file-backed log saving each event on append.

The triage verdict and the review `Decision` types come along as the vocabulary the machine records; `Retry.cause` and `Modify.findings` are strings until validate returns. Validate and review are caller functions: the coordinator writes the validate summary to `validation.json` and passes review the JSON read back from it. `stage_coordinator` sits above the numbered stages and may import every one of them, and nothing imports it. The capability experiment runs a catalog entry through the coordinator with its example program as a sink-only build, to an accepted task.

The design is cut from draft #9993, and the base is #10081.

🤖 Holistic review of 60ea1545890268d253f7411248f906095c491268.

This PR adds `stage_coordinator`: an event-folded item machine, an in-memory log with a JSON terminal store, and adapters that run triage, author, build, validate and review over the #10081 build DAG. The design is coherent, and the 130 taskforge and capability tests pass locally. There are no blockers. Three structural issues remain: one storage fault still spends revisions, the author protocol cannot carry the model errors it is meant to handle, and the transition table is configurable with no caller and permits tables the adapters cannot run.

**Should fix**
1. `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage_coordinator/coordinator.py:346` `except Exception` still records a storage fault as `BUILD_FAILED` when the fault raises `ValueError`. `RLEnvBuildStepStore.load` raises `ValueError("Blob … does not match its digest")` on a corrupted blob (`stage40_build/step_store.py:155`, covered by `test_a_blob_altered_on_disk_is_refused`), and a truncated memo raises a pydantic `ValidationError`. Neither is an `OSError`. Revisions leave the keys of unchanged steps unchanged, so every re-authored program hits the same bad memo, and the item ends `REJECTED(BUDGET)` permanently even though the program is fine. This is the case the earlier correctness comment raised and the body's "a storage fault … fails in place" claim, and only its `OSError` half is fixed. Replacement: have `step_store` raise an `OSError` subclass (or `BuildInfrastructureFailure`) for an unreadable or mismatched memo. Alternatively, reuse the frame analysis `_build_failure_line` already does and spend a revision only when the traceback passes through a program frame or the error is a `BuildFailure`.
2. `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage30_author/author.py:55` `Author.__call__` is synchronous, while `ModelClient.complete`/`complete_structured` and `llm.structured.complete_structured` are `async`. `StructuredOutputError` and `ModelUnavailable` reach the author only from those coroutines. The coordinator calls the author synchronously inside its running loop (`coordinator.py:288`, `:311`), so a model-sampling author cannot await its client. `asyncio.run` there raises `RuntimeError`, which fails the item instead of producing `AUTHOR_FAILED`. The new `AUTHOR_FAILED`/`AUTHOR_FAILURE` path is exercised only by sync fakes that raise those errors directly (`test_pipeline_walkthrough.py:490`, `:532`). Replacement: make `Author` (and `Triage`/`Review`, for parity with `Build`/`Validate`) `async def __call__`, await it in `_author` and `_authored_program`, and make `static_author` return a coroutine function. Doing this now keeps the author PR from changing the protocol under every caller.
3. `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage_coordinator/coordinator.py:157` The `transitions` field, the `table` parameter threaded through `transition`/`derive_state`, `check_transitions` and `CLOSING_EDGES` (`item_machine.py:156-184`) have no caller outside `test_a_caller_table_re_targets_an_edge_and_a_table_missing_an_exit_is_refused`. `check_transitions` also accepts tables the adapters cannot run. For example, `(TRIAGE, ACCEPT) -> BUILD` passes the check, and then `_authored_program` raises `ValueError(... not the authored None)` on every launch and relaunch, because no `AUTHORED` event set `program_digest`. Replacement: keep `DEFAULT_TRANSITIONS` as the module's single table, then delete the field, the `table` parameters, `check_transitions`, `CLOSING_EDGES` and that test. Add configurability when a second table exists, with the adapter preconditions it needs.

**Tests to drop**
4. `test_the_stage_functions_carry_the_proposal_to_an_accepted_draft_when_called_directly` (`test_pipeline_walkthrough.py:276`): guard mirroring and redundancy. `accept` returns a constant. The `run_build`→`load_draft` round trip is already covered by `stage40_build/test_run.py:183-202`. The next test (`test_run_item_records_an_event_per_stage…`) calls the same functions through `run_item`. It fails only when the fixture program changes.

**Related PRs**
5. #9849 (draft, `taskforge/10-loop`, with #9850 and #9789 stacked on it) adds an earlier `taskforge.loop.run_item` with an event log, which this PR replaces. Merge this PR first, then close #9849 and rebase or close its stack. #9993 is the reference draft and is not a merge candidate. #10092 touches only `llm/structured.py` and is independent.

🤖 Holistic review of 5a8af84889b082d1455b95b516c708561236a094.

> **In short:** This PR adds `stage_coordinator`, which runs an item through triage, author, build, validate and review as an event log. This head also makes every stage function async. The four earlier findings are fixed. One blocker remains: an `OSError` from the program's own code fails the item in place, so the author never gets a revision.

### System
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph coord["taskforge.stage_coordinator"]
    caller["StageFunctions"]:::added
    machine["item_machine: TRANSITIONS, derive_state"]:::added
    log["event_log: JsonEventStore"]:::added
    run["coordinator.run_item"]:::added
  end
  subgraph stages["taskforge stages"]
    triage["stage20_triage.accept"]:::added
    author["stage30_author: Author, AuthoredProgram"]:::changed
    review["stage60_review: Decision"]:::added
    loader["stage30_author.loader: load_program_source"]:::added
    build["stage40_build.run_build"]
    store["stage40_build: RLEnvBuildStepStore"]:::changed
  end
  caller -->|"stage functions"| run
  machine -->|"next stage from the folded events"| run
  log -->|"restore the log, save it at a terminal"| run
  run -->|"await"| triage
  run -->|"await, write authored/k/program.py"| author
  run -->|"await on validation.json"| review
  author -->|"source read back from program.py"| loader
  loader -->|"program, digest checked"| build
  build -->|"memo hit or StoreCorruption"| store
  classDef changed fill:#fde7c8,stroke:#e8710a,stroke-width:2px
  classDef added fill:#d7f0dd,stroke:#1e8e3e,stroke-width:2px
```

### Why
#10081 added the build DAG and the step store, but nothing runs an item from a proposal to an accepted or rejected task. The PR states the goal: run each stage with functions from the caller, bound the revisions and retries, and resume a failed item at the stage that raised. The design comes from draft #9993, and it replaces the earlier draft loop in #9849.

### Current state
At the merge base (d690a2a, the merge of #10081), taskforge has `stage30_author` and `stage40_build`. `Author` is a synchronous Protocol that returns an `RLEnvBuildProgram`, and `static_author` wraps a program written by hand. `run_build` runs the steps, memoizes each one in `RLEnvBuildStepStore`, and writes `draft/task.json` and `draft/provenance.json`. Only tests call it. The runner attaches the step name to a `BuildFailure`. Other exceptions, `OSError` included, pass up unchanged. `RLEnvBuildStepStore.load` raises `ValueError` for a blob that does not match its digest. The numbered packages have no triage, validate or review types.

Nothing sequences the stages, records what an item did, bounds the author's revisions, or resumes an item after a crash.

### How
**The item state is a fold over its events.** Each adapter returns an `ItemEvent` with an exit, `TRANSITIONS` gives the next stage, and `derive_state` folds the log again on each relaunch.

```python
# lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage_coordinator/coordinator.py
async def _advance(item: _Item, state: ItemState) -> ItemState:
    while True:
        event = await ADAPTERS[state.stage](item, state)
        state = transition(state, item.log.append(event))
        if state.terminal is not None:
            return state
```

**The coordinator spends the budget when it records the event.** `_failure_attrs` selects revise or reject, and `_decision_attrs` selects retry or abandon, so `transition` reads no budget. `AUTHOR_FAILED` (a `StructuredOutputError` after the repair turn) and `BUILD_FAILED` share `build_revisions`.

**Only a failure that the author can fix spends a revision.** The loom-oa-dev correctness thread asked for this split. After the earlier holistic review, `StoreCorruption(OSError)` adds a corrupt memo or blob to it. Item 1 shows that the `OSError` part is too wide.

```python
# lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage_coordinator/coordinator.py
    except (BuildInfrastructureFailure, ModelUnavailable, OSError):
        raise
    except Exception as error:
        attrs = {
            **_failure_attrs(item, state, error, _build_failure_line(error, program)),
```

**The build loads the program from the file that the author call wrote.** `_author` writes `rounds/<n>/authored/<k>/program.py`, with `k` the failures so far. `_authored_program` loads it with `StageFunctions.load_program` and compares its digest with the `AUTHORED` event. A program without source makes the build call the author again.

**The log is saved once, at a terminal.** `JsonEventStore` writes `items/<id>/events.json` last. A relaunch restores it, returns at once for an accepted or rejected item, and saves a log that a failed save lost (Codex).

**All six stage functions are async.** Triage, author and review became `async def` after the earlier holistic review.

`stage20_triage/verdict.py` and `stage60_review/decision.py` add the vocabulary. `test_imports.py` adds `TOP` for the coordinator. The README documents the table and run root. With the CI command, 129 tests pass and 1 is deselected at this head. `test_stage_coordinator.py` runs `d43.culinary.scaling` to `ACCEPTED`.

### Limitations
- **Corrupt memo:** each relaunch fails at build again (`test_pipeline_walkthrough.py:524`) until an operator deletes the memo that `StoreCorruption` names. Nothing computes the step again.
- **Plain loader:** `load_program_source` (`stage30_author/loader.py:23`) runs the author's source with full builtins and any import. The PR defers the restricted loader to the author PR.
- **Crash restarts the item:** the log stays in memory until a terminal. A killed process restarts from the last terminal or triage, and calls triage and the author again.
- **Stub validation:** validate and review are caller stubs in every test. The capability run builds a program with only a sink, and review always accepts it.
- **Sourceless author:** a program without source makes the build call the author again, so that author must be deterministic. At this time, only `static_author` returns such a program.

### Review

**Blockers**
1. `lib/taskforge/src/taskforge/stage_coordinator/coordinator.py:338` treats every `OSError` as a host fault. An authored step that opens a missing file, or raises `TimeoutError` or `ConnectionError`, has a program bug. But the item fails in place at build with `build_revisions` 0, each relaunch builds the same program and fails again, and the author never gets the traceback. A scratch test with a sink that opens `/workspace/does-not-exist.txt` gave stage `build`, terminal `failed`, 0 revisions on three relaunches. The PR body states the opposite: "A build error from the program's own code, `BuildFailure` or any other exception, costs a revision." Replacement: re-raise an `OSError` only when its traceback has no frame in the program's files (the set that `_build_failure_line` computes at `coordinator.py:398`). Or catch only a `StoreError` that `RLEnvBuildStepStore` raises for its own I/O. Add a walkthrough case where a step raises `FileNotFoundError`.

**Tests to drop**
2. `test_an_item_id_unsafe_as_a_directory_name_is_refused` (`lib/taskforge/tests/stage_coordinator/test_event_log.py:49`): guard mirroring. `JsonEventStore.path` calls `check_item_id`, and `tests/stage40_build/test_step_store.py:97` already tests it with the same inputs.
3. `test_a_source_without_a_program_in_PROGRAM_is_refused` (`lib/taskforge/tests/stage30_author/test_loader.py:26`): guard mirroring of the two `ValueError` branches of a loader that the author PR replaces. The walkthrough tests cover the load path.

**Related PRs**
4. #9849 (a draft in the #9783–#9850 stack on `taskforge/NN` branches) adds an earlier `taskforge.loop.run_item`, which this PR replaces. #9786 and #9848 add `triage/verdict.py` and `review/decision.py`, which duplicate `stage20_triage/verdict.py` and `stage60_review/decision.py` in packages that `test_imports.py` refuses. Merge this PR first, then close or rebase that stack. #9993 is the reference draft. #10092 changes only `llm/structured.py` and is independent.

**Carried from 60ea1545890268d253f7411248f906095c491268**
- 1: resolved. `StoreCorruption(OSError)` (`step_store.py:66`) covers a bad memo or blob, and a walkthrough test checks it. The `OSError` catch is now too wide (item 1).
- 2: resolved. `Author`, `Triage` and `Review` are async, and the adapters await them.
- 3: resolved. `TRANSITIONS` is the only table. The `table` parameters, `check_transitions` and `CLOSING_EDGES` are deleted.
- 4: resolved. The direct-call test is deleted.
- 5: changed. #9849 and its stack are still open, and the author leaves them to their owner. Item 4 now also names #9786 and #9848.

🤖 Fixed in 102dd4651f. An `OSError` passes through as a host fault only when no traceback in its chain runs through one of the program's frames (`_raised_in_program`, on the file set `_build_failure_line` already computes); one raised by the program's code is recorded as `BUILD_FAILED` with the program line first and spends a revision. topics.title: [grug] Hero vibe-check samples pre-switch checkpoints with the current model config
topics.body:
The hero completions sampler stamps every discovered checkpoint with the current `HERO_MODEL_CONFIG`, so after the 16K context switch (#9615) a rebuilt or re-released sample store would sample checkpoints from before step 257553 with `qk_mult` 1.48 instead of the 1.3 they trained with. Nothing flags the mismatch, because `model` is excluded from `sample_id`.

Requests already in the store are safe: `SampleStore.save_request` writes a request only once, and the stored requests for steps 246000, 252000, and 257553 record `qk_mult` 1.3 and `max_seq_len` 4096. The risk appears only when `spec.release` is bumped (the documented backfill knob) or the store root changes.

`sampling_model()` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/ops/vibe_check/config.py` should choose the model per checkpoint. `hero_checkpoint_paths` already reads each ancestor run's W&B config and could carry its `model` along; alternatively the context history could record `qk_mult` per phase.

Found in the independent review of the 16K deploy PR.

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 16K context with qk_mult 1.48
topics.body:
Switch the hero from 4K to 16K context with `qk_mult` 1.48 on all layers. The new run `hero-ctx16k-step257k` forks `hero-mfu30-step231k` at its permanent `step-257553`, where the parent stopped on 2026-10-13. Tokens per rack per update, the 390251-step schedule, and the optimizer stay the same, so the batch drops from 11264 to 2816 sequences on 11 racks.

`HERO_MODEL` gets `max_seq_len=16384` and `qk_mult=1.48`. `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES` records the 4K phase ending at step 257553, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is 1.7792877262736668e24, the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` 257552 (`global_step` 257552). `trigger_hero.sh` hands off from `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-mfu30-step231k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-257553` (permanent, `metadata.json` step 257553) and forks W&B at `hero-mfu30-step231k?_step=257552`; `current_run.py` names the child.

`build_ladder_run` now uses the checked-in history for d6144 by itself instead of relying on `main()`, and it refuses an explicit `num_steps` while a history is in effect, because the prior phases' data stages are rebuilt from the schedule length. The diagnostics launcher and restore benchmark take their default batch from the hero's tokens per rack at the model's context length (256 sequences per rack at 16K); the old fixed 1024-sequence default would have put four times the hero's load on a rack. `HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE` is replaced by `HERO_TOKENS_PER_RACK` and `hero_rack_batch_size` in `hero_recipe.py`.

In 100-step arms at 16K from permanent `step-252000` on the 11 hero racks (#9615), the dropless eval loss after step 252100 was 1.81349 at `qk_mult` 1.3, 1.81156 at 1.48, 1.81200 at 1.58, and 1.81282 for 1.68 on the global layers only. The differences are within eval noise, so we keep the YaRN-style value 1.3 × (0.1·ln 4 + 1). Those arms also ran the 16K dropless eval on 11 racks at 123.4 GiB peak memory, about 30.6% MFU, and a drop fraction falling to about 1.2e-3.

A dry build of the exact `trigger_hero.sh` launch gives 16K, `qk_mult` 1.48/1.0, capacity 1.15, batch 2816, eval at the training length every 3000 steps, `FlopsBaseline(257553, 1.7792877e24)`, and a rebuilt 4K phase with stages [0, 108000, 312192] at batch 11264. The optimizer config is identical to main's 4K build and to the parent's logged config, and the rebuilt phase's mixture, shuffle, and seed match what the parent trained with. An independent review found no blockers; its findings are fixed here except the vibe-check sampler, filed as #10100.

- Run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb` right after merge. Until the child exists and logs its config, the hourly completions workflow fails at `hero_checkpoint_paths`.
- The parent stopped at the handoff, so there is no same-batch control window. The agreed gates: the first logged step is 257553 and cross-entropy stays below 1.25 over the first 10 steps; cross-entropy in 1.09–1.15; MFU at least 29% after warmup; drop fraction below 2e-3 by step 257633–257652; peak memory 123–124 GiB; no retries, watchdogs, or runtime errors; the first 16K eval at step 258000 completes.
- Rollback relaunches `f2bc69bf6c` under `hero-mfu30-step231k`, which resumes `step-257553`.
- Eval packs at 16K from the child onward, so the `eval_dropless/*` series step down at the switch, and `eval_regressed` may fire once.
- Comparison report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Hero-16K-cutover:-hero-ctx16k-step257k-trial--VmlldzoxODEwNzE3Mg==

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Start grading in the grader workspace
topics.body:
The grading machine now starts in the grader's workspace unless its environment specifies a `working_directory`. This restores the behavior before #10021 when the environment names no directory and preserves an explicit directory when it does.

Since #10021, every script-graded task has failed while creating its grading machine on Iris. `_grade_staged` previously passed `workdir=grading.workspace`; the move to `prepare_machine_spec` dropped that argument. When the grader environment names no directory, `prepare_machine_spec` retains the spec's workdir, which is empty for an image machine because `rolloutengine._machine_spec` leaves it empty. Docker interprets an empty workdir as the image's `WORKDIR`, so laptop grading continued to work. Iris instead runs `mkdir -p ""` and fails:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The Taskforge ladder dry run on cw-rno2a hit this failure in every grader sandbox. Solver and control machines were unaffected because `draft.requirements` names `/workspace`.

A test checks the spec passed to the factory with and without an explicit `working_directory`; the grader-workspace case fails on main. The ShellSim-backed taskcompendium suite passed locally. The bubblewrap-backed tests require Linux, and CI runs the full suite.

topics.title: [shellbox] Keep ShellSim usable after command timeouts
topics.body:
The ShellSim backend closed the machine whenever one command exceeded its `command.timeout`, because the simulator's interpreter thread cannot be interrupted, and every later call then raised `Machine is closed`. In the Taskforge adversary trials of the generate-1000 run, one slow computation by the agent lost the rest of its session: 58 trials ended as unclassified and were retried to abandonment between 08:00Z and 10:00Z on 2026-10-14. Inside the simulation `sleep` costs no wall time, but CPU work does, and the wall clock does not advance, so both a heavy computation and a clock-based loop reach the timeout.

The machine now stays open, and every operation that touches the simulation is bounded by its caller's own deadline. A command with a timeout, or a shell action with a `wait`, waits for the timed-out command under the lock and runs once it ends, so two operations never run on the one-threaded simulator at once; past its own deadline it reports `TIMED_OUT` (or `RUNNING` for a shell action) and the machine stays usable. An operation with no deadline of its own, an upload, a download, or a command without a timeout, is refused at once while a timed-out command is still running, which is what those operations got before through the closed machine, and succeeds again once the command ends. A command that never ends therefore leaves the machine as unusable as before, with each later operation either timing out under its own deadline or refused immediately, never waiting without bound.

The test runs a simulated shell loop past a short timeout and checks that a transfer is refused while it runs, that a later command with a deadline completes, and that the transfer succeeds afterwards; a second test does the same through the persistent shell's `execute`. On main the first command's timeout closes the machine and both fail.

topics.title: [levanter] Repair DPO exports and explicit-mesh sharding
topics.body:
Full-model DPO on current main has three handling gaps. First, the HF export cadence is wrong: the separate-reference export hook fires on the legacy step counter, so exports land on the wrong updates and the final update can be missed or saved twice. This registers the hook on completed optimizer updates and makes the forced final save idempotent, with the interval-final naming semantics documented.

Second, the export path cannot produce serving-ready DPO artifacts: no dtype control, no tokenizer revision pinning, an always-Auto CPU mesh that breaks explicit-mesh Snowball and MoE models, and reference-code copying that breaks on URL-like checkpoints while risking trained-weight overwrite. This adds export_dtype (bfloat16 halves artifact size), name@revision tokenizers, explicit CPU meshes for explicit-mesh models, and URL-aware code copying with unconditional weight protection; the DPO save path exports only the policy subtree since the reference copy is frozen scaffolding.

Third, explicit-mesh sharding is dropped by framework and model reshapes, breaking context-parallel training, and the jagged store returns stale slices for repeated row-0 batches. This threads sharding through each reshape (including the one-line Haliax companion the grad-accum fix depends on) and fixes the row-0 offsets.

Validation is numerical parity on explicit meshes, byte-exact export round-trips, a no-double-write cadence tripwire, and row-0 regression tests: 101 passed with 1 device-gated skip, plus both 8-device Snowball tests.

Part of #10040.

topics.title: [rl] Support separate reference roles and remote artifact steps
topics.body:
SkyRL role planning on current main cannot express a separate reference footprint: colocation is hardcoded, capacity accounting ignores reference GPUs, backend YAML checks duplicate topology concerns, and a Megatron forward/train microbatch mismatch allocates GPUs before failing. This promotes policy/reference colocation to validated topology fields with footprint and capacity checks, removes the superseded YAML checks, rejects microbatch mismatch before submission, and updates every role-plan call site plus the SkyRL lock so the isolated launcher resolves on all platforms.

Remote artifact steps are broken in the lazy framework: a RemoteCallable is not directly callable for local runs, the lowered spec drops remote metadata, and Iris submissions double-write the step record. This unwraps the callable for local execution, preserves remote-ness in the spec, and skips the redundant record write on the submit path.

The RL coordinator also lacks the dedicated Daytona keys, so rollout and eval workloads cannot use separate credentials. This forwards DAYTONA_RL_API_KEY and DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY alongside the existing key.

One known gap: the Iris double-write guard has no direct test yet.

topics.title: [iris] Move Kubernetes sandbox exec and lifecycle off the controller
topics.body:
#10118 cuts the cw-rno2a controller's per-sandbox work for #10111, but sandbox commands still run through the controller. Each shellbox command is a unary `ExecInContainer` RPC. The controller authorizes it, reads its SQLite database, and opens a Kubernetes `pods/exec` websocket with a fresh TLS session inside its own process (`exec_in_container` in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/attempts.py`, `CloudK8sService.exec` in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/service.py`). Sandbox start also waits on the control tick, which creates pending pods in `K8sTaskProvider.sync` after listing every managed pod. All of this shares one Python process with 64 RPC handler threads, 128 exec threads and 8 shared SQLite read connections.

On 2026-10-14, with ~1,150 live sandboxes and 47 exec/s, a py-spy capture of GIL holders on the controller showed the lock held 82% of the time: 29% pod-list deserialization, 22% sandbox start polling and 19% exec. #10118 removes most of the first two and cuts execs per shellbox command from about 6 to 1. Controller work still scales with the command rate. At 10,000 sandboxes and today's per-sandbox rate that is about 400 exec/s, each with a TLS handshake, on one interpreter. Free-threaded Python would not remove this cost: `lib/iris/pyproject.toml` requires Python below 3.14, several C extensions would need requalifying, and the SQLite writer stays serial.

Proposed direction, in stages:

1. After #10118 deploys, measure at ~1,150 and ~2,150 sandboxes: GIL share by category, exec p50 and p99, control tick duration, and `LaunchJob` latency. If exec stays under ~10% of GIL time and the tick under 10 s at 2,000 sandboxes, stage 3 can wait behind stage 2.
2. Inside Iris: replace the per-tick pod LIST (about 28 MB of JSON per tick at 1,200 pods, repeated by the terminal-pod GC and storage-health loops) with one watch-backed pod cache. Give sandbox pods an `ownerReference` to the coordinator's pod, so Kubernetes garbage collection removes them with the coordinator pod independent of the Iris database. Replace start polling with a server stream or long poll. Reuse one `IrisClient` per shellbox factory; today each sandbox builds its own.
3. Add an exec gateway Deployment with persistent sessions. A controller call such as `ResolveExecTarget(task_id)` checks ownership once per sandbox and returns the pod name, pod UID, gateway address and a short-lived capability bound to that attempt. The gateway holds the `pods/exec` permission, verifies the capability and the live pod UID, and keeps one exec session per sandbox running a small command server over stdin and stdout. A command then costs one framed message, and file transfers stream over stdin and stdout without 64 KiB argv chunks. `ExecInContainer` stays for the CLI. Prototype the session framing against the controller first to settle binary stdin and hung-command handling.
4. If launch and cancel rate or tick time still limit throughput after stage 3, or the target passes ~5,000 sandboxes, add a sandbox broker. It creates pods directly, keeps per-image warm pools to hide the ~6 s gVisor start and the tick latency, and leases pods to coordinators. The controller then accounts for the broker's quota in place of each sandbox. Evaluate kubernetes-sigs `agent-sandbox` at this stage.

Alternatives considered:

- An in-sandbox daemon reached over the pod network removes the apiserver and kubelet from the command path. It needs an ingress rule from gateway pods into sandboxes, which narrows the isolation from #9816, and a binary injected by an init container. It is the fallback if the apiserver cannot hold the stage 3 sessions.
- Shellbox cannot call the apiserver directly: RBAC limits `pods/exec` only by pod name, so the coordinator would get exec on every pod in the namespace.
- Staging files through object storage would put credentials in the sandbox, which #9816 removed. Static grader files can go in the task image.

Open questions:

- How many concurrent long-lived exec websockets will the CoreWeave apiserver and kubelets sustain, and does CoreWeave rate-limit `pods/exec`?
- Can the gateway capability fit #9816's model, where a sandbox can never reach the gateway or hold the capability?
- Does Iris delete a coordinator's pod when its task ends, so that an `ownerReference` cascade fires?
- Is the sandbox NetworkPolicy enforced on cw-rno2a? #9816 notes it was not tested on a live cluster.
- Does a broker still need one Kueue Workload per sandbox, or does the broker's quota suffice?
- Are grader images varied enough that per-image warm pools would mostly be cold?

Done when: at 2,000 live sandboxes, sandbox command latency and control tick duration do not grow with the sandbox count or command rate, and sandbox pods are removed when their coordinator's pod is removed without relying on the controller database.

comments.body:
🤖 @rjpower, following your suggestion, we tried bubblewrap for Taskforge sandboxes, and for Python-only environments it takes the sandbox traffic off the controller entirely. That changes the case for stages 3–4 here.

**Fit.** In a census of generated environments (gen1000 and the current ladder runs), 93–100% of solver machines are ShellSim (no container) or plain `python:3.12-slim`. Graders use the `python:3.12-slim` grader base on 1,329 of 1,330 gen1000 drafts. The remaining apt needs are small (gawk, xxd, sqlite3, binutils, file, vim-common). Postgres and other-OS images are about 2.5% of published drafts and stay on Iris sandboxes.

**Permissions on cw-rno2a.** Shellbox's existing `LocalMachineFactory` (bwrap) does not start under `CONTAINER_PROFILE_DEFAULT`:
- containerd's AppArmor profile denies `mount`
- the nodes set `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`, so a process without `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` gets a user namespace with no capabilities, which rules out unprivileged bwrap
- seccomp is unconfined

Root-mode bwrap works with the default caps plus `SYS_ADMIN` and `NET_ADMIN` and AppArmor unconfined. `CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED` covers that, and Taskforge coordinators now run under it. Commands in the sandbox drop all capabilities and run with `no_new_privs`, without the host environment or the service-account mount, so a command that misbehaves damages only its own task. It shares the node kernel, though, so it is not a boundary against hostile code the way the gVisor `SANDBOX` profile is.

**A/B.** Both arms ran the same 88 validated drafts with 8 solver trials each, on the same code, on cw-rno2a, 2026-10-14 20:24–21:50Z. The control arm used the default profile and gVisor Iris sandboxes. The bwrap arm added `--container-profile container_profile_privileged`, which lowers grader-base machines to bwrap ([e020979425](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e020979425)).

| | Iris sandboxes | bwrap |
|---|---|---|
| Item wall, median | 599 s | 135 s |
| Sandbox time across solver trials | 132,959 s | 31,226 s |
| Verifier machine start, median | 16.8 s | 2 ms |
| Grading, median | 81 s | 0.6 s |
| Controller `ExecInContainer` calls (sampled) | ≥ 2,889 | 11 |
| Solve rate | 0.609 | 0.638 |

- Control replays matched on all 424 pairs. The solve-rate difference is within trial noise, and there is no backend bias in per-item rewards.
- On bwrap the model accounts for 82% of trial wall time and sandbox start for 0.6%.
- The bwrap arm's 11 controller execs all came from the one draft with a custom image, which fell back to gVisor.
- 85 of 88 tasks used no Iris sandbox at all.
- The controller logged no slow RPCs in either arm. gen1000 was ramping up in the same namespace from about 21:00Z, so the Iris arm's later starts (p99 74 s, 56 start timeouts) include pod-scheduling contention.

**Implications for this issue.** For environments that fit the coordinator's image plus a uv venv, the sandbox does not need to be an Iris job, and an exec gateway (stage 3) is unnecessary. Stages 3–4 then apply only to the remaining custom-image and other-OS environments, a few percent of current Taskforge traffic. Stage 2 (watch-backed pod cache) still stands for everything else on the controller.

Open follow-ups:
- A per-machine copy-on-write overlay for system directories in shellbox's local backend. Two drafts failed on bwrap because they write under `/opt`; for now the lowering sends such drafts to the container backend.
- Preparing the uv-managed interpreter once per coordinator. 51 bwrap machines took more than 5 s to start during the ramp.

topics.title: [grug] Balance attention work across batch shards in hero train step
topics.body:
The hero train step now permutes the rows of each global batch so that each batch shard gets a similar amount of attention work. Document packing gives rows very different attention costs. When rows stay in loader order, the busiest of the 64 shards does 2.10x the mean global-attention work on real 16K hero batches. All other shards wait for that shard at the next collective.

`balance_attention_rows` uses the FA4 segment bounds of each row to count its attended query-key pairs. Padding tokens do not add to this count. The function sorts the rows by this cost. Before the forward pass, it deals the rows to the batch shards in snake order. Even rounds go from the first shard to the last shard, and odd rounds go back. Each shard then keeps its rows in loader order.

Expert capacity drops the later tokens of a shard first. If each shard kept its rows in cost order, the tokens of short-document rows would be dropped first. The permutation adds one all-gather and one reshard of each per-row batch array. Every token still enters the loss and the router statistics. However, the row placement can change which assignments exceed expert capacity, so the loss can also change.

On real batches at 16K, the ratio of busiest-shard work to mean work decreases from 2.10 to 1.17 for global layers and from 1.46 to 1.05 for local layers. At 4K, the ratio decreases from 1.29 to 1.01.

We measured both arms on the same GB200 NVL72 rack, with 106 scored steps per arm. Each arm restored from hero step 240000. At 16K context, the step time decreases from 13.131 to 13.055 s/step (+0.58% tokens/s). At 4K, it decreases from 12.764 to 12.732 s/step (+0.25%). The loss stays within same-code noise of the control. The drop fraction changes by less than 3%.

The companion PR changes the FA4 mask. With both changes on a second rack, the 16K step time decreases from 13.046 to 12.833 s/step (+1.66%). In that stack, balancing alone gives +0.29%, because faster masked attention also makes the imbalance smaller.

All numbers above come from the code before two later fixes. The cost now excludes padding, and each shard now keeps its rows in loader order. We did not measure again after these fixes.

All measurements used one rack. The all-gather sends the whole global batch to each GPU, so its cost increases with the number of racks. We did not measure this cost at the 11-rack hero size.

topics.title: [levanter] Vectorize FA4 SM100 segment mask and zero accumulators in prep
topics.body:
This PR changes two parts of the SM100 FA4 kernels. The forward evaluates the document segment mask 32 columns at a time. The backward zeroes its fp32 accumulators the same way as upstream FA4 and no longer launches scalar zero-fill kernels. Before this change, the forward for document-masked local attention at hero shapes was about 1.7x slower than upstream FA4 varlen. Now the forward is within 5% of upstream.

The vectorized mask_mod builds keep-bitmasks with `r2p_bitmask_below` and `r2p_bitmask_above`. Its output is bitwise equal to the output of the scalar mask. In the backward, the preprocess kernel clears the dQ accumulator while it computes the row dot products. dK and dV start from an XLA zeros buffer that the kernel receives through `input_output_aliases`. Callers give the aliases to `cutlass_call` as a tuple of pairs, because the kernel cache key must be hashable. `cutlass_call` converts them to the dict that `cutlass.jax` expects. SM90 and SM120 keep the current zero-fill path.

Kernel measurements on one GB200 at hero shapes (median 16K rows):

| Metric | Before | After | Upstream varlen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local-layer forward | 3.16 ms | 1.96 ms | 1.87 ms |
| Local-layer fwd+bwd | 10.23 ms | 8.97 ms | |
| Projected attention cost | 0.777 s/step | 0.672 s/step | |

Output, dq, dk and dv match an fp32 reference with the same relative error as before. That error is 2.0e-3 to 2.6e-3, which is the bf16 rounding floor. The FA4 test file passes on GPU.

The end-to-end test ran on one GB200 NVL72 rack, restored from hero step 240000. At 16K context, the step time goes from 13.055 to 12.956 s/step (+0.76% tokens/s). The loss stays inside same-code noise, and the drop fraction does not change. A rank-0 trace shows that the attention kernels are 0.23 s/step faster. Peak memory increases by 0.5 GB because of the aliased dK/dV buffers.

The remaining gap to upstream is about 0.035 s/step, and it is in the backward. This backward uses 1-CTA with the scalar mask. The upstream backward uses 2-CTA.
