topics.title: [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for GPUs
topics.body:
Add a `ring_gather_combine` MoE implementation: the ring expert-parallel backend with its dispatch and combine done as gathers in both directions. `implementation=None` resolves to it on GPUs, CUDA and ROCm alike. On other backends, TPU included, `None` still resolves to `ring`, which keeps the scatter-add combine, and `moe_implementation="ring"` selects `ring` on any backend. Like the other expert-parallel implementations, it runs only on an expert mesh axis of size two or more. Without one, `moe_mlp` falls back to the local `scatter` path, so a single-device call never reaches the gather code.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)` and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. With `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true`, which RL training on H100 enables, XLA lowers GPU scatter-adds to sorts. `ring_gather_combine` builds an inverse map from each (token, k) assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the combine get custom VJPs, so activation rows move only by gather in both directions: each token sums its at most K slot rows (K = 4 in the June model). The inverse map itself is an int32 scatter-set (`ep_common._assignment_sources`, 0.04 ms at June shapes), and the routing-weight gradient still scatter-adds one scalar per slot, as in `ring`. `_moe_mlp_ep_ring_local` takes the dispatch and combine pair as an argument, and `moe_mlp` binds it when it picks the backend, so the ring code has no platform check. The default is picked by `resolve_moe_implementation` from `jax.default_backend()`, which initializes JAX. The experiment configs' `__post_init__` checks can run before `jax.distributed.initialize`, so they now call `validate_moe_implementation`, which only checks the name. The combine's profile scope is renamed from `scatter` to `combine`, the name the other EP backends use.

In bf16 the two backends round differently. `ring_gather_combine` sums each token's rows in f32 and rounds to bf16 once, in the combine and in the dispatch gradient. `ring`'s bf16 scatter-add rounds after every add, on CPU and on MI300X, so the two can differ in the last bits of a token's sum. A bf16 test checks the gather sums bit for bit against an f32 sum rounded once, on inputs whose products and f32 sums are exact. On CPU the test fails if the sums run in bf16. On MI300X it cannot catch that, because XLA on ROCm keeps the fused bf16 sum in f32. At June shapes on one MI350X (job 453908), the combine matched an f32 scatter-add rounded to bf16 bit for bit. The order of a scatter-add's f32 adds is unspecified, so other inputs can differ in the last bit.

With `implementation="ring"`, the traced program is the same as on the merge base. Exporting its forward and backward for CUDA (8-way expert parallelism, bf16) gives an identical jaxpr and debug-stripped StableHLO with the XLA `ragged_dot`, and an identical jaxpr with the Triton `ragged_dot` that H100 uses by default. Pallas Triton cannot be lowered without a GPU, so that path was compared at the jaxpr level only. The profile scope name is the only difference.

Step time with `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` and `--moe-impl` set to each backend: full June width and sequence length (hidden 2560, 256 experts, top-4, seq 4096), cut to 4 layers to fit 8x 80 GB, with 32,768 tokens per device and `recompute_all`. Each figure is the median over steps 5-24 of two fresh-compile runs per backend, alternating on one node (Iris jobs `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-b` and `/dev/ring-gather-9860-v5p8-b`):

| Hardware | XLA flags | `ring` | `ring_gather_combine` | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention | default | 0.636 s | 0.623 s | 1.9% faster |
| 8x H100, EP8, `xla_flash` attention | `--xla_gpu_deterministic_ops=true` | 3.232 s | 0.756 s | 4.3x faster |
| TPU v5p-8, EP4, `tpu_splash` attention | default | 1.064 s | 1.162 s | 9.2% slower |

Repeat runs agree within 0.4%. Losses agree within 2e-5 on H100 and are identical on TPU.

The MI350X measurements below ran on an earlier revision that chose the gather path with a ROCm check inside `ep_ring.py`. The gather code is unchanged, except that the inverse map now comes from `_assignment_sources`, which runs the same scatter-set.

Single-MI350X microbenchmark at June per-GPU shapes (`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py` from #9891, job 453908):

| | scatter-add | gather |
|---|---|---|
| combine forward | 2.420 ms | 0.969 ms |
| dispatch + combine, forward and backward | 5.436 ms | 1.790 ms |

Full June model, batch 64, flash attention, 8x MI350X, fresh compiles, step time with the gather path and the routing top-k from #9889 together:

| remat policy | before | after | jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.823 s (12.40% MFU) | 1.735 s (13.03% MFU) | 453972 / 453979 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.848 s | 1.788 s | 453841 / 453957 |

Losses agree within 4e-4. These runs used the flash attention from #9853 and the tuned Triton `ragged_dot` from #9859. This PR does not depend on either.

With the GPU default, `test_grugformer_moe.py` passes on CPU (job 461508) and on one MI350X, where the multi-device tests skip (job 461652). On 8x H100, `None` resolves to `ring_gather_combine` and every ring test passes, including the one that hangs on MI300X. 6 `ragged_all_to_all` tests fail there, the same way on `main` (Iris jobs `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-tests` and `/dev/ring-gather-9860-h100x8-ragged-ab2`). The experiment-config tests pass on CPU (job 461652). The ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py`, including `ring_gather_combine` against `ring` with capacity drops, pass on 8x MI300X (12 tests) and on CPU (9 tests; 3 in-process multi-device tests skip) in job 456128. The bf16 test and the other `ring_gather_combine` tests pass on 8x MI300X and on CPU in job 458228. With #9928 and #9880 stacked on top, the 17 ring tests pass on 8x MI300X in job 456022. Some MI300X runs hang in `test_moe_mlp_ep_backends_match_dense_value_and_gradients_when_available[all_valid-ring]`, with one GPU busy and the other seven idle. The same test hangs on `main` (job 456135: 2 of 4 runs on this branch, 1 of 4 on `main`). On 8x MI350X (job 454059) the earlier revision passed the whole file except 5 ragged all-to-all tests, which also fail on `main` (job 454060) because `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` cannot parse `gfx950` as a compute capability.

#9928 and then #9880 (`ring_dedup`) are stacked on this branch. `ring_dedup` reuses `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows`.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend
topics.body:
Add `ring_dedup`, an opt-in expert-parallel MoE backend selected with `moe_implementation="ring_dedup"`. `ring` all-gathers every token to every expert shard and reduce-scatters a full-size output. With top-4 of 256 experts over 8 shards, a token reaches 3.3 shards on average, so most of those bytes go to shards that do no work on them.

`ring_dedup` sends each token once to each GPU that owns one of its top-4 experts, through a fixed-capacity `all_to_all`. A small metadata `all_to_all` carries the combine weights and local expert ids, and a trailer row holds the sender's valid count. The expert side keeps ring's capacity rule, local assignment selection (`_select_local_assignments`, #9928) and `ragged_dot`, sums each token's local expert outputs in f32, and returns one row per token. Dispatch and sender-side combine use ring's `_dispatch_rows` and `_combine_rows` (#9860); expert-side combine uses the shared weighted gather. Neither pass uses a hidden-width scatter-add.

The sender capacity per destination is `pooled_transport_capacity_factor` times the expected distinct tokens per destination under uniform routing, scaled by the sender's valid tokens, and `moe_mlp` raises if it is unset. It reuses the `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` parameter so one benchmark flag sets the sender capacity for both backends. The capacity has no worst-case guarantee: correlated routing can drop a token's assignments to a destination that still has expert capacity. A factor of 1.1 gave no sender drops on the June benchmark (`--pooled-transport-capacity-factor`, #9852) and on uniform routing; other workloads may need another value. At batch 64 each collective moves 537 MB per GPU, against 1,174 MB for ring.

On CPU in f32, the 8-shard tests match a dense reference to 1e-5 in outputs and all four gradients with sender drops, receiver drops, both together under uneven padding with an empty sender shard, and an all-padding batch, and match ring wherever no sender drops. In bf16, `ring_dedup` also keeps the routing-weight gradient in f32. Against f32 ring on one full-shape layer on 8x H100, its outputs and gradients are within 0.47-0.52%. bf16 ring is within 0.50-0.57% except the routing-weight gradient, at 5.75%, because ring casts the routing weights to bf16. On MI350X and TPU v6e the two backends' routing-weight gradients agree to 0.17%. The full-model drop rate on MI350X is 1.00-1.12%, against 0.93-0.99% for ring.

June Snowball 67B-A2B, 8x MI350X, EP8, batch 64, flash attention, fresh compile caches:

| Remat | ring | ring_dedup | Jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.730 s (13.07% MFU) | 1.580 s (14.31% MFU) | 454012 / 454021 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.798 s | 1.688 s | 454022 / 454026 |

The MI350X ring column ran ring with the gather combine, now `moe_implementation="ring_gather_combine"`, with the ROCm routing top-k from #9889 in place. One `ring_dedup` run (job 454010) ran out of memory on GPU 7 at step 5 and hung; its retry passed. That was allocator fragmentation around the step's temp buffer, which also hits ring at batch 96, and #9901 fixes it with `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false` in the HPC Fund wrapper.

On NVIDIA `ring_dedup` is faster than the GPU default `ring_gather_combine`. On TPU it is slower than `ring`, so TPU should keep `ring`. One MoE layer at the June batch-64 shapes (262,144 tokens, uniform routing, capacity factor 1.0), forward and backward, median of 20 calls, transport 1.1:

| One layer | 8x H100 | TPU v5p-16 (8 chips) | TPU v6e-8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ring | 36.0 ms | 109.9 ms | 106.0 ms |
| ring_gather_combine | 33.4 ms | | 225 ms |
| ring_dedup | 25.6-26.1 ms | 131.6 ms | 182.7 ms |

The June model cut to 4 layers to fit in memory, batch 64, median of steps 2-19, against the platform default:

| 4-layer model | 8x H100, `xla_flash` | TPU v5p-16, `tpu_splash` |
|---|---|---|
| `recompute_all` | 0.627 s → 0.595 s (-5.1%) | 1.118 s → 1.322 s (+18%) |
| `save_moe` | 0.597 s → 0.575 s (-3.7%) | 1.043 s → 1.220 s (+17%) |

Losses match to 5 decimals in every pair. The June model does not fit on v6e-8 at 2 layers. We have not profiled the TPU slowdown; `ring_gather_combine`, which also moves rows by gather, is 2.1x slower than `ring` on v6e-8.

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

topics.title: [grug] Keep hero eval and FLOPs metrics continuous across a relaunch
topics.body:
GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len fixes the held-out eval context independently of the training context, so a run that changes context can keep scoring at 4K and its eval_dropless/* series stays comparable. The dropless eval reports evaluation start and end progress events, as the other evals do.

Per-example FLOPs rise with context length, so the cumulative throughput/total_gflops would jump at a context switch. A FlopsBaseline (completed steps and cumulative FLOPs at the handoff) adds the parent's history to the new shape's count; current MFU uses the new attention cost.

topics.title: [levanter] Add a benchmark for the Triton ragged_dot kernels
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py`, which times the Pallas-Triton grouped GEMM behind `haliax.nn.ragged_dot` on one or more GPUs. For each layout (fwd, dlhs, drhs) it times both Triton kernel families (`tile_map` and `group_grid`), XLA's `ragged_dot_general` and a dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs. Each timing is the median of repeated windows after a warmup. Rows are written as JSON lines.

With `--sweep`, the script times the tile-map kernel for every block config in a bounded grid over block sizes, warps, stages, `num_xcds` and `group_m`. `--shard i/n` runs every n-th config, so the GPUs of one node can split the grid. The AMD block-size table and the per-call numbers in #10009 came from this script on MI350X.

With `--devices N`, each implementation runs on the first N local GPUs at once, as one `shard_map` program in which every GPU computes its own copy of the case, as a training step runs the expert GEMMs from one process. Times stay per GPU, and rows record N in `device_count`. On 8x MI350X (job 461032, the w13 cases at M=16384 and 131072), every Triton and XLA row with 8 GPUs busy was within 1.2% of its one-GPU time. The same mode on #9859's jax-triton kernels (job 460977, another node) hit the jaxlib hsaco race in 3 of 6 tile-map rows and ran 0-7% slower per GPU with 8 GPUs, dense matmul included; we have not found the cause of that slowdown.

The script calls the tile-map kernels and block-config lookup that #10009 adds, so this PR is stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first. #9859 ports the same kernels to Triton launched through jax-triton, with `_tile_map_triton_call` as the tile-map entry point. Branch `levanter/bench-ragged-dot-triton-jax-triton` keeps a version of this script for that port.

On one MI350X (job 460986), the timing mode and a five-config `--sweep --shard 1/3` ran with no errors. At the June w13 shape (G=32, K=N=2560, M=16384), the tile-map kernels ran fwd, dlhs and drhs at 594, 639 and 486 TFLOP/s, against 594, 635 and 483 in #10009.

topics.title: [zephyr] Abort ThreadedBatchWriter output when the producer fails
topics.body:
When the body of a ThreadedBatchWriter `with` block raised, `__exit__` sent
the normal end-of-stream sentinel. The write function then completed, and
`write_parquet_file` committed the partial file through `atomic_rename`.
Stages that treat an existing output file as "shard done" then skipped the
shard on a re-run and kept the partial output. The normalize main/dups writer
and the datakit quality writer use this pattern.

`__exit__` now sets an abort event before it wakes the thread. The next read
of the write function's stream raises `WriterAbortedError`, so `atomic_rename`
removes its temporary file and nothing is committed. A normal close is
unchanged.

The datakit quality stage in #9694 removes partial outputs after the fact
(`_discard_outputs`); with this change, that code is not necessary.

topics.title: [levanter] Stop background iterators after completion
topics.body:
Buffered background iterators now remain stopped after the producer finishes or raises. Previously, consuming the single end marker or error left later `next()` calls waiting forever on an empty queue. Levanter uses this iterator to prefetch data loader batches and evaluation requests.

Regression tests reproduce the hang after normal exhaustion and producer failure in bounded and unbounded queues. The affected safe suite passed 1,063 tests with 13 skips.

topics.title: [haliax] Prefer XLA ragged_dot on AMD MI300X and MI325X
topics.body:
On AMD MI300X and MI325X (gfx942), `ragged_dot(implementation="auto")` now tries XLA before the Pallas Triton kernels. MI350X (gfx950), NVIDIA, TPU and CPU keep their current order. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` still overrides the choice.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X found that XLA's bf16 grouped GEMM takes 11-28% less time than the best Triton config for each fwd, dlhs and drhs triple. For example, the June w13 projection at M=131072 took 10.91 ms with XLA and 12.25 ms with tuned Triton. These numbers come from microbenchmarks only. We have not run a full-model A/B on MI300X. MI350X must keep Triton because XLA rejects bf16 `ragged_dot` on gfx950.

XLA's hipBLASLt grouped GEMM crashes with `ROCM_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` when HIP command buffers are on, so ROCm runs must pass `--xla_gpu_enable_command_buffer=`. The MI300X timings above used that flag. The Grug training entry points already set it by default, and so does the HPC Fund Slurm wrapper, `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` on `main`.

`_GpuFamily` gains an `AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` member, detected from the compute capability that ROCm reports (`"gfx942"`). gfx942 keeps the tile-map kernels and the block configs swept on MI350X, so the Triton fallback is unchanged. #9905 is stacked on this PR and reuses `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` for its MI300X block configs, so merge #10009, then this PR, then #9905.

At #9905's head, which contains this PR, the file gives 46 passed and 30 skipped f32 kernel cases on MI300X (job 458222) and 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223).

Stacked on #10009. Merge #10009 first, then retarget this PR to `main`.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [haliax] Tune tile-map ragged_dot dlhs and drhs blocks for MI300X
topics.body:
Give MI300X and MI325X (gfx942) their own dlhs and drhs tile-map blocks for the Triton `ragged_dot` kernels: 128x256x32, 4 warps, 8 XCDs, group_m=2, with 2 pipeline stages for dlhs and 1 for drhs. Until now gfx942 reused the MI350X (gfx950) blocks. gfx942 has 64 KiB of LDS per CU, against 160 KiB on gfx950, and the MI350X dlhs and drhs blocks run 20-35% slower on MI300X than the swept tile. The forward pass keeps the MI350X block (256x256x64). 128x256x32 is 16% faster for fwd at the June shape with M=16384, but no faster at M=131072 and 15-22% slower at a Mixtral-like shape.

The table is keyed on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942` from #9904. That PR makes `implementation="auto"` prefer XLA on gfx942, so these blocks apply when Triton is selected explicitly. Merge order: #10009, then #9904, then this PR.

The f32 skip in `test_triton_kernel_families_match_ragged_dot_general`, which #10009 adds for gfx942, now keys on `_GpuFamily.AMD_INSTINCT_GFX942`. Triton uses xf32 for f32 dots on gfx942, and the group-grid f32 tiles exceed the 64 KiB LDS.

Per-call microbenchmarks on one MI300X (partition `mi3001x`; jobs 454650, 454673, 454679 and 454683; sweeps 454658, 454659, 454667 and 454668) show that the tuned dlhs and drhs blocks cut a fwd+dlhs+drhs triple by 9-24%. For example, the June w13 shape at M=131072 drops from 14.67 ms to 12.25 ms.

At this branch's head, `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` gives 76 passed on MI350X (job 458223) and, on MI300X, 46 passed and 30 skipped (job 458222).

Part of #9812

Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0). ## TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09). ** Given **one expert E** ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)) built from the Snowball student B ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab)) by SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: * plain SFT on E's traces * SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT) * on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts (4x sample traces from the test set size). Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. Every arm starts from B. ## Benchmark CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop. ## Frozen evaluator Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8), vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes. **Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).** - E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms). - Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100). - RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100). - OPD: [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL), 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron). - Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction. ## Artifacts Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/skyrl/runs/p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399 @ 3e34be3f](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399/tree/3e34be3f884ff737f85354b060ea831ce0c90636) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`), RS-SFT [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282 @ 073d128c](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282/tree/073d128cb1e53652126cce37a7cc2c96625d3c80) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`), OPD [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75 @ 9d189320](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75/tree/9d1893207226cf72f701187e1d5260d9fc3c931d) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`). Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals//record.json` (every record id is in the final comment's ledger). GPU-hour method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298. ## Not in scope Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval). ## Decision log - 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher. - 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used. - 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain. - 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm. - 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris. - 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

comments.body:
🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval SFT, LR 1e-5, 3 ep) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.123 | 0.30 | 0.27 | 0.31 | 0.022 | 0.41 | 41.2 | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.05 | 0.68 |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.094 | 0.24 | 0.21 | 0.25 | 0.015 | 0.34 | 34.5 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.71 |
| OPD update 75 | 0.035 | 0.12 | 0.077 | 0.12 | 0.006 | 0.060 | 20.3 | 0.08 | 0.12 | 0.12 | −0.32 |

Reading:
- Everything is a small perturbation: no checkpoint moves more than 0.13% of B's weight norm overall, and the largest component change is the expert's attention at 0.65%.
- The expert (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 1,454 rows) concentrates its change in attention, the router and the LM head and leaves the MoE expert MLPs almost untouched (0.047%, 13% of weights changed). The two SFT transfer arms (LR 1e-6, 4 epochs, 1,500–1,600 rows of the expert's text) do the opposite: they move the expert MLPs 4–6× more than the expert did and touch 35–41% of all weights. OPD moves least of the three arms (0.035% overall, comparable to the expert) and touches 20%.
- Direction: none of the arms re-creates the expert's weight change. The cosines between an arm's delta and E's delta are 0.05–0.12 in attention and the expert MLPs (random directions in this dimension give ≈0). The one shared direction is the LM head, where plain SFT and RS-SFT align with E (cosine 0.68 and 0.71) while OPD moves the LM head the opposite way (−0.32). Recovering the expert's CruxEval score therefore does not require copying its weights; three different weight changes produce it.
- RS-SFT changes the weights less than plain SFT (0.094% vs 0.123% overall) while scoring higher; it trains on fewer, verifier-correct rows.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights. Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

From a task interference standpoint, this seems like it would favor OPD; smaller magnitude changes, much closer frobenius norm to the original expert update, and fewer weights changed overall -- despite that it gets roughly comparable skill transfer.

@karansag

> much closer frobenius norm to the original expert update

Yes, but the direction seems almost orthogonal (0.08 here, 0.05 in  #9984 )? So it doesn't seem like it's making a "similar" update in that sense. 

The simple retained tasks we used here (GSM8K, Math500, and GPQA in #9984 ) didn't show much regression, though. Small drop in IFEval-Instruct on #9984.  SFT w/rejection sampling showed what seems like a significant improvement in GPQA-D, actually. 

If there are known typical examples of interference, we could test on that, but maybe it's fine so long as we watch retained task performance?

topics.title: [grug] Move ring's local assignment selection into a helper
topics.body:
The next PR in this stack, #9880, adds a `ring_dedup` expert-parallel backend that selects each GPU's local expert assignments exactly the way `ring` does. This PR moves that selection into a shared helper first, so `ring_dedup` can call it instead of copying it.

`_select_local_assignments` in `ep_ring.py` covers the per-expert counts, the prefix capacity cap, the top-k selection ordered by (local expert id, flat position) and the padding of the `ragged_dot` group sizes. The computation moves without edits, so ring's behavior is unchanged. The existing ring tests in `test_grugformer_moe.py` pass on 8x MI350X (9 tests) and on CPU (6 tests; the 3 multi-device tests skip), in job 455432.

Stack, in merge order (each PR is based on the one before):
1. #9860 [grug] Add a ring EP backend without activation scatter-adds for ROCm (base `main`). It also edits `ep_ring.py`, so this PR sits on top of it.
2. #9928 this PR (base `grug/rocm-ring-combine-top-k`, #9860's branch)
3. #9880 [grug] Add a token-deduplicated ring_dedup expert-parallel MoE backend (base `grug/ring-select-local-assignments`, this PR's branch)

topics.title: [rl] Select PivotRL pivots from frozen-policy pass rates
topics.body:
This PR implements a few of the key components from the NVIDIA's [PivotRL paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.21383).

**PivotRL in a nutshell:**
1. make a bunch of `(trajectory, turn): (context up to turn) -> teacher action` tuples (I usually call this `long` or `melted` format).
2. generate `k` roll-outs from a frozen student at each of those points
3. grade them using "functional" verifiers
4. identify "pivot" turns -- ones that have non-zero reward variance and are meaningfully difficult
5. (... single-turn RL...)
6. ???
7. profit

**This PR is split into 4 commits, I recommend reviewing in that manner.**
1. add original nemotron graders
2. add datasets, initial data pre-processing and prediction code
3. prediction post-processing/filtering
4. add openhands dataset & grader for a novel experiment (I added this separately, to give a flavor for what it's like adding a new pivotRL task--tbd if any of this helps).

### Agent Generated

Build PivotRL's training data in Marin as artifact steps: candidates, pass rates under a frozen policy, then the pivots that Eq. 5 of the PivotRL paper selects (0 < passed < K and pass rate below λ), written as `train.parquet` in the candidate schema. Each λ and selection criterion is a small artifact over the same pass rates.

Candidates come from three releases. `marin.rl.nemotron_pivot` turns NVIDIA's SWE and Terminal pivot releases into one candidate per expert turn of each trajectory's longest row, keeping earlier turns' reasoning as `reasoning_content` and dropping NVIDIA's pass-rate fields; `experiments/datasets/nemotron_pivot.py` publishes them as `processed/nemotron-pivot-{swe,terminal}-long`. Validation holds out whole SWE instances (100) and Terminal tasks (30) by hash bucket and keeps four evenly spaced turns per held-out trajectory, about 500 rows each, since a trajectory's rows share almost their whole prompt. OpenHands candidates are prepared from `nebius/SWE-rebench-openhands-trajectories@3545538`: one row per expert tool call in a resolved trajectory, with the working directory replayed from earlier bash observations.

`marin.rl.pass_rates.measure_pass_rates` serves the policy with vLLM, sends one `n=K` chat request per row so each prompt is prefilled once, and grades every reply with a `PassRateTask` returning a verifyit `Reward`. Every grading component is its own column (`c_<name>` per sample, `passed_<name>` per row), so selection can switch criterion without resampling. Context overflows, persistent request failures, and grader errors exclude a row rather than scoring it 0. Rows commit in atomic chunks, so a rerun samples only missing chunks, and `config.json` refuses to resume under a different config. Every run sets `enable_thinking` explicitly: SWE and Terminal think, matching prompts that carry the teacher's reasoning; OpenHands does not, since its teacher never thinks. Grug runs keep special tokens so graders can strip its `<|start_think|>` block.

The graders live in verifyit. `nemotron_pivot.grade_tool_call` scores SWE replies with NeMo Gym's word-overlap argument match (the reward), the PivotRL paper's tool-name-only match, and an exact-argument match. `grade_terminus` ports the string-only Terminus-2 verifier, parsing the reply after any reasoning. `openhands_next_action` grades by what a call does and to which paths, so `cat core.py` from the package directory matches viewing `widgets/core.py`; pairs the rules cannot settle go to an LLM judge only when one is configured. MarinSkyRL computes training rewards with the same algorithms but pins the standalone verifyit repository, so sharing these graders there needs that pin moved to `lib/verifyit`.

This replaces profiling inside MarinSkyRL's generate entrypoint, which reached 63-79 samples/min on 16 H100s while vLLM ran 2-10 of 16 sequences, because each request group waited on single-writer trajectory retention.

Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05 smoke runs on one 8xH100 node each, the first 64 candidates per dataset and K=8 (seed 1), graded all 1,536 replies with no exclusions:

| dataset | thinking | replies that think | passes / 512 | pivots |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SWE | on | 462 | 113 (tool name only: 264) | 24 |
| Terminal | on | 181 | 20 | 9 |
| OpenHands | off | 0 | 280 | 40 |

On SWE, the prompt length vLLM reports is within 10 tokens of a local render that includes earlier reasoning and about 490 tokens above one without it, so the reasoning reaches the model; Terminal and OpenHands match exactly. Grug's thinking never leaks into tool-call arguments.

topics.title: [grug] Route QBRoutedMoE through the jax_triton top-k kernel
topics.body:
QBRoutedMoE now selects experts with `levanter.grug._moe.topk.top_k_indices`, called per token shard inside `shard_map`, in place of `jax.lax.top_k`. That is the jax_triton kernel from #9830, which the hero model already uses. `jax.lax.top_k` still handles rows of 1,024 or more (XLA:GPU runs its own top-k kernel on those), non-float32 inputs, non-GPU backends and environments without jax-triton.

On AMD, jax-triton 0.3.1 with triton 3.6.0, Levanter's GPU pins, compiles the kernel for ROCm with jaxlib 0.11.1 or newer. jaxlib 0.11.0 never loads `jax_rocm10_plugin`'s Triton launcher, so there the kernel falls back to `jax.lax.top_k`.

Time per call in ms, from 16 calls on distinct inputs in one executable, median of 5 runs. The shapes are the router logits per call of the hero model and of the June Snowball model:

| shape, k | GPU | `lax.top_k` | jax_triton (this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | GB200 | 0.837 | 0.0754 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | H100 | 1.107 | 0.0954 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI300X | 0.847 | 0.0665 |
| [65536, 384], 9 (hero) | MI350X | 1.000 | 0.0570 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | GB200 | 0.229 | 0.0207 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | H100 | 0.308 | 0.0238 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI300X | 0.351 | 0.0246 |
| [32768, 256], 5 (June) | MI350X | 0.402 | 0.0167 |

The AMD rows ran on jax 0.11.1, jax_rocm10_plugin 0.11.1+rocm10.1.0, jax-triton 0.3.1 and triton 3.6.0, with the AMD HPC Fund cluster's ROCm 7.2 libraries on the library path, as `experiments/amd/hpcfund/run_gpu.sh` leaves them. The `lax.top_k` baseline depends on that: with only the wheel's own ROCm libraries loaded, `lax.top_k` on MI350X takes 2.4 ms (hero) and 1.7 ms (June), while the kernel times do not change. The kernel code is unchanged since #9830; the NVIDIA rows are earlier measurements of it with the same harness.

On NVIDIA, the models that use QBRoutedMoE (`experiments/grug/moe`, `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp` and `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe`) now run the kernel, because Levanter's GPU extra installs jax-triton. In the optimized HLO of the June training step on H100 and GB200, the 4 `sort` ops of main's routing become 2 `triton_kernel_call`s, and the all-gathers, all-reduces and reduce-scatters are unchanged. Step time does not change measurably. June model at full width with 4 layers and sequence length 4096, ring expert parallelism over the node, `xla_flash` attention and XLA `ragged_dot`; median of steps 2-19 per run, runs alternating between main and this PR:

| GPU | Tokens per GPU | Runs per side | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4x GB200 | 8,192 | 4 | 0.5742 s (0.5723-0.5759) | 0.5740 s (0.5719-0.5760) |
| 8x H100 | 16,384 | 5 | 1.457 s (1.403-1.508) | 1.513 s (1.336-1.539) |

On H100, step time varied between runs of the same code: main's five runs spanned 1.403-1.508 s (7%) and this PR's 1.336-1.539 s (15%). Five runs per side cannot separate the two. Scaled to these shapes, the per-call times above put the saving below 0.1% of a step. At 16,384 tokens per GPU on GB200, runs of both variants intermittently hung in a training step or ran out of memory, so those runs are left out. TPU step time was not measured; there `top_k_indices` falls back to `lax.top_k` inside the same `shard_map`.

On MI300X and MI350X the kernel's indices equal those of `lax.top_k` computed on the CPU, for widths 37 to 1,023 and k up to 37, on random, tied, constant, ±0, ±inf and NaN rows. ROCm's own `lax.top_k` ties -0 with +0 and orders NaN payloads differently, while the kernel follows XLA:CPU and CUDA. The GPU tests therefore check the kernel's output against `lax.top_k` run on the CPU backend.

The AMD venv recipe in `experiments/amd/hpcfund/README.md` still installs jaxlib 0.11.0 without jax-triton, so runs from it silently keep `lax.top_k` until that recipe moves to 0.11.1.

Supersedes #9889, which added a separate ROCm-only Pallas kernel for power-of-two widths.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launch use the carry-offload memory budget
topics.body:
`trigger_hero.sh` passed `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.75` and `--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor=85` to the hero coordinator. Since #9831, `_apply_hero_ep_runtime_defaults` gives the hero's carry-offload configuration a 0.78 memory fraction and slop factor 105 together with `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading`. Explicit values take precedence over those defaults, and `run_grug` copies the coordinator environment into the training tasks, so a hero launched from main would compile with 0.75 / 85 and host-memory offloading on. On one GB200 rack restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint, that combination aborts compilation on every rank in `HloRematerialization` (`hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118`, `Check failed: !place_before_list.empty()`).

Without the two overrides the launch resolves to 0.78 / 105 with host-memory offloading, the configuration measured in the #9831–#9834 rack benchmarks. The live hero is unaffected: Iris retries reuse the bundle it was launched with.

Follow-up to #9831.

topics.title: [eval] Iris retries overwrite completed run records
topics.body:
An Iris retry can reuse an evaluation's serialized `EvaluationIdentity.run_id` and `output_dir`. The replayed Evalchemy process then appends samples and overwrites `record.json` under an already sealed result URI. A tracker link can therefore change its score after it has been sealed.

Reproduce:
1. Submit an evaluation batch through `experiments/evaluation/launch.py` and let an Evalchemy process finish and seal its FineStore archive.
2. Cause Iris to classify the parent task or Evalchemy child task as retryable after that write, such as a post-completion `PodDeleted` or worker preemption.
3. Observe that the replay has a new Iris attempt or child-job ID but writes to the original FineStore path and run-level `record.json`.
4. Compare the first completed attempt, replayed attempt, and current record at that URI.

Expected: an Iris retry must preserve completed results as immutable artifacts. It should either skip a successfully sealed evaluation or allocate attempt-specific run IDs and output paths. A later failed attempt must not downgrade or replace an earlier succeeded record.

Confirmed examples:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261003-210313-Aleph-Alpha-Kolibri-1-mbppplus-b75b/results` first completed at 262/378 (`0.6931216931`). A parent-task retry ran a second MBPP+ child against a new serving endpoint and wrote 274/378 (`0.7248677249`) to the same path. The current `record.json` and FineStore view report the second score.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20261002-002728-laion-snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203-gpqa-diamond-5b7b/results` changed from `0.636` to `0.5993265993` after a parent `WORKER_FAILED` retry replayed GPQA-Diamond against a new serving child.
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260930-085011-arcee-ai-Trinity-Mini-nupa-9a91/results` held a sealed 5,000-item attempt with 2,414 correct answers (`0.4828`). Iris classified the completed Evalchemy child attempt as `WORKER_FAILED` after `PodDeleted`, retried the same task and path, and the final canonical record became `0.4788`.
- The Kolibri retry also changed MATH500 from `0.984` to `0.992` and HumanEval+ from `0.774` to `0.7682926829` under unchanged result URIs. When the retried parent was later killed, several earlier succeeded Kolibri `record.json` files were rewritten as `infra_failed`.

`_run_id()` is evaluated while constructing the batch in `experiments/evaluation/launch.py`; Iris retries replay the serialized batch. `write_record()` in `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/records.py` then writes unconditionally to `{prefix}/{run_id}/record.json`.

topics.title: Add aligned Snowball checkpoint merging and calibration
topics.body:
Add aligned Snowball/Grug checkpoint merging and coefficient/curvature calibration. Parent tensor names, shapes, dtypes, and expert identities must already align; the tools do not infer expert permutations.

Constrained exports preserve the original input checkpoint's (Base) metadata, tensor layout, and at least 75% of its scalar weights bit-for-bit. A temporary incomplete marker blocks Marin checkpoint reads until the actual change cap passes and the audit is saved outside the checkpoint and read back. Successful finalization removes the marker, preserving Base's original file inventory. Every serial stage is checked against original Base. The historical unconstrained exporter remains available separately.

Calibration uses one pinned runtime launcher with an explicit module selection and optional hash-verified SkyRL patch. Chunk allocation preserves each trainer's scoring and tie ordering.

The [Campaign 2 artifact archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/tree/1ef199578aeec9f08e142a8dd760d44658264be4/campaign2-recipes) contains 54 recipes and [unrounded result evidence](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/1ef199578aeec9f08e142a8dd760d44658264be4/campaign2-recipes/results-evidence.json) for 48 completed candidates. The [evaluation release](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/inputs/RELEASE.md) records the BFCL/NUPA evaluation commands. DARE-TIES-02 scored 45.53 BFCL and 0.00 NUPA200 while changing 6.04% of Base parameters. Non-target retention was not evaluated. Broader benchmark comparisons are recorded in #9975. topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---

## Campaign 4 follow-up: constrained routed-expert transfer

### TL;DR

Campaign 4 tested 71 audited merges that transfer routed-expert rows from Reference-KL Step20 into Antidoom Step12. All 355 fixed-policy evaluation records completed. `adaptive-delta-08` led with a **220.40** four-target sum versus Base's **174.90**, while changing **9.47%** of Base's scalar weights. Its scores were 83.54 HumanEval+, 74.07 MBPP+, 34.33 OlympiadBench, and 28.46 BFCL-Parity; MATH500 was 93.60 versus Base's 95.00.

The top three candidates all used layer-adaptive donor deltas with coefficients above 1.0. Exact donor-row transfer did not match them: the best wide-support serial merge reached 204.66 while changing 27.77% of Base. The result supports selective, task-weighted delta extrapolation for this parent pair. It does not establish broad retention: the four transfer benchmarks selected the checkpoints, MATH500 was the only regression canary, and all scores are single runs.

### Public checkpoints

1. [`adaptive-delta-08` — Target Sum 220.40](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-08-2026.10.14/tree/2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a), revision `2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a`
2. [`adaptive-delta-05` — Target Sum 213.49](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-05-2026.10.14/tree/4a19865c0ed69efab0bf457804d2d698fb3f72f5), revision `4a19865c0ed69efab0bf457804d2d698fb3f72f5`
3. [`adaptive-delta-06` — Target Sum 213.48](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-06-2026.10.14/tree/337eb566795323f93ee16bbf294da6efd5e48539), revision `337eb566795323f93ee16bbf294da6efd5e48539`

Each repository contains the evaluated weights, OpenMDW 1.1 license, exact recipe, original-Base readback audit, protocol, final tracker, and sanitized copies of the five sealed evaluation records. The repositories are public and ungated; the links above pin immutable revisions.

### Experiment design

Base was [Antidoom RLVR1 Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e). The extraction target was [Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647). The selection objective was the unweighted percentage-point sum of HumanEval+, MBPP+, OlympiadBench, and BFCL-Parity. MATH500 was a regression canary and did not enter selection.

A merge could change at most 30.00% of Base's indexed scalar weights. Only rows of routed-expert gate, up, and down projection tensors were eligible. Every other weight and every non-weight file had to remain byte-for-byte identical to Base. Serial stages were measured against original Base, so an intermediate checkpoint could not reset the budget. The full public protocol is [here](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-08-2026.10.14/blob/2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a/provenance/campaign4/PROTOCOL.md).

The campaign covered eight method families: DARE-linear; serial DARE-TIES followed by ISO; targeted serial transfer; task-paired serial transfer; exact task-union transfer; layer-adaptive delta transfer; behavioral-residual grafting; and wide-support serial transfer. The initial 20 candidates reused Campaign 2's seed-0 R25 routed-expert support. Later candidates used fixed BFCL, HumanEval+, and MBPP+ routed-expert rankings. Construction wrote a temporary incomplete marker, materialized the candidate, read every stored object back, checked the support and actual-change limits, verified unchanged bytes outside support and across non-weight files, wrote and reread the external audit, then removed the marker.

Evaluation used the pinned October 2026 Marin policy: Marin `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, Evalchemy `958cdb8019b7a4c8432fe85eb9572538ceb75950`, and Harbor `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. Each candidate used one eight-H100 vLLM server shared by its five evaluations. The suites contained 164 HumanEval+ tasks, 378 MBPP+ tasks, 30 OlympiadBench tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity trials, and 500 MATH500 tasks. A score sealed only when at least 90% of declared trials were scoreable.

The implementation and reproduction guide are in [PR #10135](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10135). Run the merge commands from the immutable [Campaign 4 implementation revision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/14a407e045f83f38e4e94a2fb21869707a256997). Exact public replay artifacts are available for the three published checkpoints. For the remaining 68 candidates, the tracker publishes scores and recipe summaries; exact recipes and sealed record contents are not public, so exact byte-for-byte replay of the full search is not possible from public artifacts alone.

### Results

`adaptive-delta-08` recovered 64.08% of the extraction target's aggregate improvement over Base. By benchmark, it recovered 78.12% of the HumanEval+ gap, 84.40% of the MBPP+ gap, 44.98% of the OlympiadBench gap, and 59.57% of the BFCL-Parity gap. MATH500 fell 1.40 points.

The search showed three useful patterns:

- Exact transfer did not improve monotonically with breadth. Exact-union family scores ranged from 188.64 to 200.65; wide serial scores ranged from 195.64 to 204.66 while changing 20.19%–27.81% of Base. Interference at wider supports is one plausible explanation, but this sweep does not isolate its cause.
- Task-specific support was useful, but serially composing exact supports did not add their gains reliably. The best task-paired result was 198.60, and the best targeted serial result was 198.73.
- Layer-adaptive scaling produced the only candidates above 207.77. Its top three changed 8.18%–9.47% of Base, less than half the changed fraction of the widest exact transfers.

These comparisons are retrospective maxima from unequal family sizes. They isolate useful construction patterns for this parent pair; they do not estimate statistical uncertainty or performance on unmeasured tasks.

### Complete tracker

Scores are percentages. Target Sum is HumanEval+ + MBPP+ + OlympiadBench + BFCL-Parity using unrounded component scores. Merge time includes checkpoint construction and the original-Base readback audit. The tracker abbreviates the `bfclparity-pi` suite as BFCL-Parity.

topics.title: [analysis] Independent pre-registered forecast of the hero's final loss, with 80/95% intervals
topics.body: Hi @ClassicLarry @dlwh, To add uncertainty to the Aug 19 pre-registration in #8435, I made an independent forecast of the hero's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss` (4K eval packing). It is frozen at 58% of training and uses only public data. **Result:** median **2.035**, 80% interval [2.023, 2.047], 95% [2.016, 2.054]. The Aug 19 pre-registration (2.039) sits at our 68th percentile, so the run looks on track for it. A finish near 2.10 looks very unlikely. **Method in brief** - The ladder is used only for the remaining drop from now to the end. The level comes from the hero's own post-swap evals, which makes the forecast nearly independent of the floor E. - Backtests set the drift persistence, the method error and an allowance for distance-dependent bias. They use held-out ladder rungs and the 67B-A2B run (#6044). In nested leave-one-out, the 80% intervals cover 14–15 of 16 held-out cases. - PTB gets its own term because of its noise and the exposures in #9874. A PTB-free companion target is forecast too: 2.047 [2.036, 2.059]. **One finding:** most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap comes from counting lm_head FLOPs in compute. On the H100 d768–d1536 runs, excluding them moves the fitted floor from 1.913 to 1.573 and the forecast from 2.116 to 2.037 (see the comment below for the refit's exact setting). **Pre-registration, code and scoring rules:** https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/prereg-v2-2026-10-09/preregistration_v2.md - The scoring rules were fixed in advance, including what happens if the context or the schedule changes. - This is v2. I revised v1 (median 2.045) the same day after re-auditing its backtests, on the same data. Both versions are tagged, and every change is listed. - I'll post a check-in at 70% and the scored comparison after the run ends.

topics.title: [post-training] Transfer two Snowball experts at once: MOPD, mixed SFT, mixed SFT-RS and weight merging
topics.body: Follow-up to #9920. That experiment moved one expert's gain back into the Snowball student B. This one builds a second expert in a different domain and asks whether both experts' gains can be moved into B at once, and what it costs in the other domain (forgetting) and on unrelated benchmarks (collapse). Full record, every evaluation id and the cost ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850. ## Setup - **Student B**: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab). - **Expert E** (CruxEval, from #9920): [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). - **Expert E₂** (MMLU-Pro): B fine-tuned with E's recipe (full SFT, AdamH 0.9/0.95, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, frozen router bias, 32 H100, 60.6 H100-h) on 1,359 correct [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) traces over a seeded subset of 1,606 MMLU-Pro test questions; the other 10,426 questions were never trained on and serve as a probe. Browse the GLM, E and E₂ traces side by side: https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/ (public). [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254 @ acb97183](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MMLUPro-Expert-E2-Step254/tree/acb97183af633533df4f4f63d83adc1e0a7a9748) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task157-e2/checkpoints/karan/e2-mmlupro-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.09.1/hf/step-254`). - **Evaluator** (frozen, same as #9920): Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking on, unseeded sampling at temperature 1.0. MMLU-Pro is scored on the 1,606-question training subset and separately on the 10,426 held-out questions. Intervals are 95% bootstraps over problems or question groups, one evaluation pass unless stated. ## Arms All arms start from B and use the same 3,206 prompts (1,600 CruxEval + 1,606 MMLU-Pro); AdamW LR 1e-6, 4 epochs, one checkpoint per epoch, final checkpoint kept unless a target metric dropped with the interval excluding 0. | Arm | What it trains on | Selected checkpoint | |---|---|---| | Mixed SFT | sample 0 of every prompt from E's and E₂'s k=8 demo pools (3,206 demos) | step 803, [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedPlain-SFT-Step803 @ 1a0bcf70](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedPlain-SFT-Step803/tree/1a0bcf70fa4b599701d5e0c9f0864452d531a9dc) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task165-mixed/checkpoints/karan/mixed-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.10.2/hf/step-803`) | | Mixed RS-SFT | first execution-correct (CruxEval) or answer-correct (MMLU-Pro) sample per prompt (2,903 demos; uses verifiers the other arms do not have) | step 727, [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedRS-SFT-Step727 @ 95dd3f4a](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MixedRS-SFT-Step727/tree/95dd3f4ab7487a67907b5a22748a2c2bc77770cc) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task166-mixed/checkpoints/karan/mixed-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.10.1/hf/step-727`) | | MOPD | on-policy distillation, B's rollouts scored by E on CruxEval prompts and by E₂ on MMLU-Pro prompts (MarinSkyRL, 2 epochs = 100 updates, 7 × H100x8) | step 100, [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MOPD-Step100 @ 4bb97259](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-MOPD-Step100/tree/4bb972592c0094d51d29321f9af2a6defa2ccea1) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-mopd2-cruxeval-mmlupro-2ep/exports/global_step_100/policy`) | | Merge | B + a·(E − B) + b·(E₂ − B) at a = b = 0.5 and 1.0, and TIES (d = 0.5), with the #9974 tools; no training | TA 0.5: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Merge-TA0.5 @ 07001c33](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Merge-TA0.5/tree/07001c3333337bdea61647c74bcb227f60310fa6); TIES: [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Merge-TIES-d0.5 @ ffb5b685](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Merge-TIES-d0.5/tree/ffb5b68590fdf7c5fe01351a332e7915d574bc61); TA 1.0 not published (regressed); S3 sources `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/mopd2/merges/{ta-a0.5-b0.5,ta-a1.0-b1.0,ties-d0.5-a1.0-b1.0}/r3/` | ## Results | Model | CruxEval in / out | MMLU-Pro subset / held-out | GSM8K | MATH500 | GPQA-D | IFEval inst-strict | Training H100-h | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | B | 55.4 / 57.8 | 44.5 / 44.1 | 90.4 | 89.8 | 41.9 | 81.1 | — | | E | 79.4 / 71.4 | 60.3 / 59.8 | 92.1 | 92.2 | 44.8 | 78.9 | 35.9 | | E₂ | 54.5 / 52.9 | 66.4 / 64.0 | 93.9 | 90.4 | 47.6 | 80.2 | 60.6 | | Mixed SFT (803) | 75.4 / 71.5 | 62.4 / 62.9 | 93.4 | — | — | — | 122.0 | | Mixed RS-SFT (727) | 77.3 / 77.3 | 68.2 / 64.8 | 94.1 | 92.4 | 57.6 | 78.3 | 93.6 | | MOPD (100) | 82.1 / 76.4 | 64.2 / 64.4 | 92.8 | 90.0 | 47.5 | 80.0 | 557.9 (+28.3 exports) | | Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 76.5 / 67.6 | 63.2 / 61.6 | 93.9 | 92.0 | 47.1 | 79.0 | 0 (CPU) | | Merge TIES | 72.8 / 68.1 | 61.4 / 60.8 | 92.3 | 90.0 | 47.3 | 81.8 | 0 (CPU) | | Merge TA a = b = 1.0 | not run | not run | 50.0 | invalid record | 30.0 | 73.3 | 0 (CPU) | Paired comparisons (pp, 95% bootstrap): - **RS-SFT vs MOPD**: RS higher on the MMLU-Pro training subset, +4.0 [+1.6, +6.3], but not on the held-out questions, +0.4 [−0.5, +1.4]; MOPD higher on CruxEval input, +4.9 [+1.6, +8.1]; CruxEval output unresolved, RS − MOPD +0.9 [−2.1, +3.75]. - **Against the experts**: both finals are above E on CruxEval output (MOPD +6.1 [+2.9, +9.4], RS +7.0 [+3.75, +10.4]) with input differences unresolved; on the MMLU-Pro subset MOPD − E₂ = −2.2 [−4.5, +0.1] and RS − E₂ = +1.7 [−0.5, +4.2]. Intervals that include 0 do not establish equivalence. - **Plain mixed SFT** is below RS-SFT by 5.8 [3.5, 8.2] on the MMLU-Pro subset and below E on CruxEval input. - **Merging** at half strength beats B in both domains with no training but stays 8–10 pp below the trained arms on CruxEval output; at full strength it regresses badly on GSM8K and GPQA-D with runaway generations. - **Collapse checks**: GSM8K at or above B for every trained arm; MATH500 and GPQA-D at or above B on the RS-SFT and MOPD finals (RS-SFT's GPQA-D 57.6 is +15.7 [+10.4, +21.0] over B, one evaluation, reported without interpretation); IFEval 1–3 pp below B (RS −2.8 [−5.2, −0.2], MOPD −1.1 [−3.6, +1.2]). ## Reading Two experts can be moved into B at once: both RS-SFT and MOPD improve both domains over B and land at or above each expert in that expert's domain on the point estimates. The two methods trade off by domain and are not matched controls for each other (RS-SFT had verifier access, 8 teacher samples per prompt and a different token budget; MOPD cost 6× more H100-hours). Plain SFT recovers less; merging is a cheap partial substitute at half strength only. ## Caveats - One evaluation pass per checkpoint except the stated repeats; plain SFT's 803-vs-603 selection used two passes each. Intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons or checkpoint selection. - Both primary targets are test-exposed (training-is-test); the held-out MMLU-Pro questions are an additional probe, never a selection input. - The RS-SFT demo selector used an older answer-extraction rule than the evaluator: 14 of its 1,400 MMLU-Pro demos are wrong under the evaluator's rule, 15 prompts would have been gained and 1 lost, 45 would have used a different sample. Reported as trained; no corrected run. - Two records (B and MOPD-100 on MMLU-Pro) had a retried evaluation attempt; all numbers come from each record's pinned FineStore manifest (an earlier reading gave B 43.9 and MOPD 65.3 on the subset). - Evaluation infrastructure cost 1,752.6 H100-h of serve time, 894.5 of it in 31 groups that produced no record (serves left running on stale endpoints, #10030). ## Links | | | |---|---| | Full report with record manifest | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984#issuecomment-6144923850 | | Single-expert experiment | #9920, https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 | | Record manifest (machine-readable) | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/records-manifest-20261013.json` | | Canonical MMLU-Pro labels and subset | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/mmlupro-canonical-v2/` | | GLM traces and captured prompts | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/glm-bench-traces/` | | Demo pools | `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/teacher-traces/mopd2/` | | MOPD config | https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/76fc4be980aff1b14a42bfa549b5fe7479744701/cloud/iris/configs/snowball_mopd2_cruxeval_mmlupro.yaml | | Merge tools | https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974 | | GPU-hour method | https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298 | | Trace browser | https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/ | Weights are being uploaded to Hugging Face under open-athena; the S3 paths above will be replaced by HF links as each lands.

🤖

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages; cosines are given against E and against E₂.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Expert E₂ (MMLU-Pro) | 0.035 | 0.64 | 0.043 | 0.067 | 0.15 | 0.11 | 12.9 | 0.21 vs E | 0.37 | 0.06 | 0.38 |
| Mixed plain SFT step 803 | 0.180 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.42 | 0.033 | 0.53 | 56.3 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.40 / 0.50 |
| Mixed RS-SFT step 727 | 0.171 | 0.38 | 0.38 | 0.40 | 0.030 | 0.49 | 54.7 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.06 / 0.06 | 0.02 / 0.02 | 0.42 / 0.51 |
| MOPD update 100 | 0.045 | 0.13 | 0.099 | 0.12 | 0.008 | 0.084 | 25.2 | 0.05 / 0.05 | 0.11 / 0.13 | 0.07 / 0.07 | −0.14 / −0.15 |
| Merge TA a = b = 0.5 | 0.031 | 0.53 | 0.041 | 0.064 | 0.13 | 0.11 | 12.1 | 0.71 / 0.69 | 0.82 / 0.82 | 0.60 / 0.56 | 0.78 / 0.71 |
| Merge TIES d = 0.5 | 0.043 | 0.73 | 0.057 | 0.084 | 0.19 | 0.14 | 17.2 | 0.73 / 0.69 | 0.75 / 0.73 | 0.73 / 0.65 | 0.84 / 0.69 |

Reading:
- The two experts are built the same way and look the same: 0.035–0.036% of B's norm overall, change concentrated in attention (0.65%), router (0.15–0.17%) and LM head, expert MLPs nearly untouched, 13% of weights changed. Their deltas share a direction (cosine 0.21 overall, 0.37 in attention, 0.38 at the LM head) while their expert-MLP changes are nearly independent (0.06), consistent with a common change in how the model answers (both experts start using their reasoning block on far more prompts) on top of domain-specific MLP changes.
- The mixed SFT arms move the weights most (0.17–0.18% overall, 55–56% of weights changed, expert MLPs 0.38–0.40%), 5× more than the experts whose text they train on, and in a direction almost orthogonal to both experts' deltas (cosine ≈0.02 overall and in the expert MLPs; 0.06 in attention). Only the LM head aligns (0.40–0.51).
- MOPD moves the weights a quarter as much as the SFT arms (0.045% overall, 25% of weights changed), again nearly orthogonal to the experts (0.05–0.13), with the LM head moving against both experts (−0.14 / −0.15). It recovers both experts' scores anyway.
- The merges are, by construction, the experts' deltas: TA 0.5 is their average (cosine 0.69–0.71 with each, magnitude 0.031%), TIES keeps the larger of the two per weight (0.043%, attention 0.73%). They sit far from where the trained arms end up (cosine between merge and arm deltas not computed here).
- Net: four different weight changes, differing in size by 5× and nearly orthogonal in direction, all land within a few points of the experts on both domains. The transfer is not a recovery of the expert's parameters; it is a re-learning of the behaviour from a different starting direction, which is also why the arms' off-domain scores (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA-D, IFEval) do not simply track the experts'.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights (two values = vs E / vs E₂). Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.
